Not a house, but the main surviving monument of a Barishal zamindar family; the Department of Archaeology listed it together with Ulania in 2019. Not on the project's research list.

architectural_style: Twin math (memorial towers), about 80 ft high, on three acres.
preservation_status: Enlisted by the Department of Archaeology for preservation in March 2019; in an erosion-affected area and described as near ruin.

Not a house, but the main surviving landmark of the Madhabpasha zamindari and the usual starting point for visiting it; recorded separately as the revised list recommends.
established_era: Dug in 1780 (Bangladesh Tourism Board, Adar Bepari, Daily Star 2016).
founder_or_family: Raja Shivnarayan of Chandradwip (Madhabpasha). Named after Rani Durgavati, but sources differ on who she was.
architectural_style: Large tank with a wooded island in the middle and ghats on three sides; about 46 acres (Daily Star 2016).
preservation_status: Maintained as a public park/tourist site (district tourism list).

Not on the project's research list; found in a Daily Star report (2019). It is a possible candidate for the list's unsourced 'Satani Zamindar Bari' in Banaripara, but nothing links the two.
established_era: About 300 years old, per a descendant (Daily Star 2019).
founder_or_family: Zamindars Bija Ram Saha and Sita Ram Saha, who came from Jashore.
architectural_style: Compound of ten residences and temples; two houses and five temples remain.
preservation_status: Near collapse and overgrown; no archaeological survey. Descendant Dhruba Saha lives in the 'Boro Bari'.

name_bn: গৌরনদী জমিদার বাড়ি (জমিদার মোহন লাল সাহার বাড়ি, আশোকাঠী)
alternate_names: Mohan Lal Saha Bari; মোহন লাল সাহার বাড়ি; Prasanna Bhaban; প্রসন্ন ভবন; Ashokathi Zamindar Bari; Lal Mohan Saha's house (Chandpur Times list)

short_description: The family house of zamindar Mohon Lal Saha at Ashokathi, about 1,000 feet from the Gournadi upazila headquarters on the Gournadi-Mirerhat river (a branch of the Arial Khan). Its large Durga temple of about 1850 is the main feature. In 1971 Pakistani troops and Razakars looted the house, burned the servants' quarters and smashed the temple's rooftop lions. This identifies both the master list's vague 'Gournadi Zamindar Bari, Ashokathi' and its extra entry 'Mohan Lal Saha Bari / Prasanna Bhaban'.
established_era: About 150 years before 2011, i.e. mid-19th century; the Durga temple was built around 1850 (bdnews24 blog 2011).
founder_or_family: Zamindar Mohon Lal Saha; the temple was built by his father Prasanna Kumar Saha. Mohon Lal lived in the building called Prasanna Bhaban.
architectural_style: Not described beyond a large Durga temple about 30 x 20 yards with 45 pillars and once lion statues on the roof, and a stone-paved pond in front.
preservation_status: Deteriorating in 2011: cracked roofs, falling plaster, leaks. Durga Puja is still held. Heirs alleged a land-grab attempt and asked for state protection.

alternate_names: Koloshkathi Zamindar Bari; Kalaskathi; Tero Zamindarer Bari (house of the thirteen zamindars); তেরো জমিদারের বাড়ি
coordinates_note: Pin found in Google Maps on 15 Oct 2026. Matched 'Kalaskathi Jomidar Bari' (heritage building, 105 reviews, plus code G9F9+Q7C, Shahebganj-Kalaskathi Rd), which fits the district portal's route via the Sahebganj ferry. touristplaces.com.bd gives 22.702921, 90.346597, about 20 km north, which is wrong for this site and was not used.
short_description: An old settlement in Bakerganj known for its thirteen zamindar households, all descended from Janakiballabh Roy Chowdhury. The district portal describes the main manor near the government primary school beside Kalsakathi Bazar, another decaying house beside it, and a temple with a large courtyard where Jagaddhatri Puja draws crowds each November-December. A Shiva temple with black-stone images still has worship.
established_era: Early 1700s (district portal; Ajker Patrika 2022); 'late 17th century' in the master list and Daily News Reel (2020).
founder_or_family: Janakiballabh Roy Chowdhury, younger son of Ramakanta of Garuria. After his elder brother Ramballabh plotted to kill him, he fled to Murshidabad, where the Nawab made him zamindar of Arangpur pargana, and settled at Kalsakathi. The thirteen zamindar branches are his descendants. Last zamindar per Daily News Reel: Rajeswar Roy Chowdhury, who left for Kolkata after 1947.
architectural_style: A village of brick zamindar houses, compared with Panam Nagar; the main house is over 300 years old, brick and lime with terracotta work (district portal; Daily News Reel).
preservation_status: In ruins and unprotected: the main house is structurally standing but overgrown; one family still lives in part of it (Ajker Patrika 2022; district portal).

alternate_names: Lakhutia Zamindar Bari; লাখুটিয়া জমিদার বাড়ি; Lakutia Rajbari

Google's address does not settle the Barishal Sadar vs Babuganj question.
short_description: Seat of the Roy (later Roy Chowdhury) family of Lakutia, a Brahmo zamindar family linked by marriage to the Tagores. The family founded Rajchandra College and the Pushparani Institution and built the Lakutia road and canal (Daily Star 2025). The house was used as a freedom fighters' training camp in 1971 (BSS 2022). After decades of decay under BADC custody, the Department of Archaeology restored its structure in 2025-26, and it is about 5 km from Durga Sagar.
established_era: Family estate founded by Rupchandra Roy; the main house was built or enlarged by his grandson Rajchandra Roy. Dates differ: 'the 1700s' (Daily Star 2025), '17th century' (Daily Star 2019), 'early British period' (Daily Star 2016), 'around 1600 or 1700, per locals' (BSS 2022).
founder_or_family: Rupchandra Roy (family founder); Rajchandra Roy (builder of the main house). Later members: Pyarilal Roy (barrister, Brahmo), his sons aviator Indralal Roy and boxer Pareshlal Roy; last zamindar Debendra (Deben) Lal Roy Chowdhury, who moved to Kolkata.
architectural_style: Two-storey brick mansion with nine rooms, 25.40 m long, 9.20 m wide and 8.20 m high (Prothom Alo and BSS 2025-26), with three ghat-lined ponds called 'Babur Pukur' and a row of Shiva temples on the west side (Daily Star 2016).
preservation_status: Department of Archaeology restoration began 4 May 2025; phase one (foundation, brickwork, Satkhira clay-tile roof, Tk 60 lakh) was reported complete in January 2026 (BSS). Phase two (doors, windows, floors) had not started. The grounds are held by BADC, whose warehouse stands beside the house; the government has acquired about 8 acres and a large pond.

alternate_names: Chandradwip-Madhabpasha royal seat; Makhan Rajar Bari; Raja Satindra Narayan's house
coordinates_note: Pin found in Google Maps on 15 Oct 2026. Matched 'Madhabpasha Raja Bari' (historical landmark, only 1 review, plus code Q77J+32C), about 1 km west of Durga Sagar. No separate 'Chandradwip Rajbari' place exists. Thin match; confirm on site.
short_description: The zamindar house at Madhabpasha, 300 m north of the Bakla-Chandradwip Rajbari ruins and the later seat of the Chandradwip Raj, one of the oldest ruling houses of southern Bengal. After a cyclone and Magh raids, Kandarpanarayan moved the capital to Madhabpasha around 1584; the estate became a Mughal zamindari in 1611, defaulted after the 1793 Permanent Settlement and was auctioned in 1799, and the family's remaining share ended with the 1950 abolition. A brass cannon over five cubits long bearing Kandarpanarayan's name was kept at the capital (Banglapedia). Durga Sagar Dighi beside it has its own record.
established_era: Chandradwip (Bakla) was a pre-Mughal principality; Kandarpanarayan moved its capital from Kachua to Madhabpasha around 1584 (Bangla Banglapedia). After Raja Ramchandra submitted to the Mughals in 1611 it became an ordinary zamindari. English Banglapedia says Madhabpasha became the head kachari of the former Raj from the early 19th century.
founder_or_family: Dynasty: Danujamardana Deva by tradition (Banglapedia calls the story doubtful); Basu line from Paramananda Basu; Kandarpanarayan and Ramchandra. Zamindars after 1611 include Kirtinarayan, Premnarayan, Udaynarayan (Mitra), Shivnarayan, Lakshminarayan and Jaynarayan.
architectural_style: Surviving pieces per Bangla Wikipedia and Parjatan Bichitra (2025): a six-room building said to date from the 1800s and a two-storey Durga temple. Not described further.
preservation_status: Bangla Banglapedia says the Madhabpasha zamindar house and nearby Ramsagar Dighi are protected by the Department of Archaeology. Present condition not reported.

short_description: The Roy Chowdhury house at Shyampur, Rangashree union, listed on the union's government tourism page. In 1971 it served as an operational headquarters and camp for 300-400 freedom fighters; Natubabu was attacked in September 1973 to stop him testifying against war criminals and died on 10 October 1973 (Daily Observer 2019). Prothom Alo has also reported calls to preserve it as a Liberation War memorial (article seen in search, not read). The master list's 'revenue and administration centre' text is unsourced.
established_era: Not documented in the sources checked.
founder_or_family: Roy Chowdhury family; the Daily Observer (2019) names the late zamindar Kumud Bandhu Roy Chowdhury, whose successors own it. Natubabu (died 1973) lived there.
architectural_style: Not documented; described only as a palace with historic residential buildings on about seven acres.
preservation_status: Near ruin; the family still lives there and reports pressure from land grabbers (Daily Observer 2019).

alternate_names: Ulania Chowdhury Bari; উলানিয়া চৌধুরী বাড়ি
coordinates_note: Pin found in Google Maps on 15 Oct 2026. Matched 'Ulania Jamidar Bari' (historical place, 326 reviews, plus code VJ54+FQ9). No place is named 'Ulania Zamindar Bari Mosque'; 'Ulania Jame Mosjid' (52 reviews, 22.8584481, 90.608212) is about 130 m away and is probably, but not certainly, the zamindar mosque.
short_description: The Chowdhury zamindars' seat at Ulania on the Meghna-Arial Khan estuary. The district portal and 2019 reports trace the family to Muhammad Hanif, a Mughal soldier posted against the Magh and Portuguese pirates. River erosion has swallowed most of the roughly 100 buildings; what survives is the fortified house section, the Ulania Zamindar Bari mosque and a pond, enlisted for protection by the Department of Archaeology in 2019.
established_era: Mughal period; Bangla Wikipedia says about the 1700s. The Daily Observer (2019) puts it in the 16th century but under Aurangzeb, which is inconsistent.
founder_or_family: Muhammad (Subedar) Hanif, a soldier of Persian descent who came with Mughal commander Aga Mehedi to suppress Magh and Portuguese pirates and settled with a patta from the emperor (district portal via Bangla Wikipedia; Daily Observer and Dhaka Tribune 2019, citing local historian Sirajuddin Ahmed).
architectural_style: A complex of brick buildings with a 'castle' section, a mosque and a pond; English Wikipedia says the zamindars built about 100 buildings over 300 years.
preservation_status: Listed by the Department of Archaeology for preservation in March 2019. Most of the complex has been lost to Meghna erosion; the castle section, mosque and pond survive and remain threatened (Daily Observer 2019).

alternate_names: Abdul Jabbar Mia Bari; আব্দুল জব্বার মিয়া বাড়ি; Abdul Jabbar Mia Zamindar Bari
coordinates_note: Pin found in Google Maps on 15 Oct 2026. Matched place 'জব্বার মিয়া জমিদার বাড়ি' (listed as a housing society, plus code FPQG+7FR, Kunjerhat Bazar). short_description: The house of the Chowdhury family of Kutuba union, Borhanuddin, built in stages in the early 20th century by Abdul Jabbar Mia (Chowdhury) on land the family had held since Barket Ullah dug a large pond to settle the place. The property was bought from the Bakerganj District Board in 1927, confirmed by a Calcutta court in 1931 and endowed as waqf in 1337 BS; Abdul Jabbar Government College (1972) stands on about 50 acres of the waqf land. Several news features since 2020 call it a zamindar house of Bhola.
established_era: Built in phases between 1319 and 1351 BS (about 1912-1944), per English Wikipedia; the family's first brick house was built earlier by Jibon Hawladar.
founder_or_family: Abdul Jabbar Mia, later Chowdhury (1255-1341 BS, about 1848-1934), a landholder with about 4,000 acres, descended from Dhan Gazi, who settled in Manika. Son Mojibur Haque Chowdhury sat in the East Bengal Legislative Assembly (1954); grandson Reza-e-Karim Chowdhury (Chunnu Mia), a language-movement activist, was elected in 1970.
architectural_style: Two- to three-storey house of brick, surki, iron and wood with 12 decorated rooms, in traditional zamindar style (English Wikipedia).
preservation_status: Standing and lived in by descendants (English Wikipedia, citing reports from 2020-2025).

alternate_names: Borhanuddin Zamindar Bari; Chowdhury Bari, Borhanuddin; চৌধুরী বাড়ি; Borhan Uddin Chowdhury Bari
coordinates_note: Pin found in Google Maps on 15 Oct 2026. Matched place 'বোরহানউদ্দিন চৌধুরী বাড়ি' (listed as a housing society, 1 review, plus code FM8Q+JR). 'Borhanuddin Chowdhury Bari Jame Mosque' (mosque, 7 reviews) is about 240 m west at 22.4665995, 90.6871873.
short_description: The family seat of the Chowdhury (Hawladar) zamindars after whom Borhanuddin upazila is named, in Sachra union. Wikipedia, citing the Daily Sangram and Jaijaidin, describes a two-storey house, three kachari buildings and a mosque at the gate, with much of the land the zamindar gave for public use now occupied. Banglapedia lists the Chowdhury Bari mosque among the upazila's relics. The project's first research list attached a 1748 founding by Haider Ali and a three-storey house to this entry; those details belong to the separate Haydar Ali Zamindar Bari (Haydar Mahal) in Kutuba union, recorded as haydar-ali-zamindar-bari-haydar-mahal.
established_era: About 150 years ago according to the Daily Sangram report cited by Wikipedia, i.e. mid to late 19th century; the Wikipedia infobox says c. 1950, which conflicts.
founder_or_family: Zamindar Borhanuddin Chowdhury, who held about 27 mouzas and land in Bhola and Barishal (Bangla Wikipedia). English Wikipedia's upazila page says Borhanuddin Hawladar, son of the Kalaiya zamindar Khairullah Hawladar, bought the Kaliganj area, which became 'Borhanuddin Hawladar's Haat' in 1872 and gave the upazila its name.
architectural_style: Two-storey brick, surki and rod residence with three kachari buildings used for estate business, hearings and guests, and a mosque at the entrance (English and Bangla Wikipedia).
preservation_status: Much of the complex is at risk from neglect; the mosque is in fairly good condition because it is still used (Wikipedia).

A talukdar was a lesser landholder, below a zamindar.

founder_or_family: Vromon Guide attributes it to 'a zamindar named Borhanuddin' who owned 27 mouzas; its local name points to a Talukder named Jinnatulla. Unresolved.
architectural_style: A main house with a notable hall room, smaller houses around it, a large dighi and a mosque to the north-east (Vromon Guide).
preservation_status: Descendants still live there; the house has lost much of its beauty through lack of upkeep (Vromon Guide).

alternate_names: Haydar Mahal; হায়দার মহল; Haider Ali Zamindar Bari; Kutuba Zamindar Bari; কুতুবা জমিদার বাড়ি
coordinates_note: Pin found in Google Maps on 15 Oct 2026, from the place's own pin. Matched place 'হায়দার আলী জমিদার বাড়ি' (historical landmark, 2 reviews, plus code GPC2+JWH, 'located in Manikar Hat Bazar'); 'Haydar Mahal' and 'হায়দার মহল' open the same pin. short_description: Called Haydar Mahal after its builder, the three-storey house of zamindar Haydar Ali at Pet Manika in Kutuba union, Borhanuddin, begun in 1155 BS (about 1748). It still holds deer antlers, peacock feathers and a tiger skin, and some family items are in the National Museum. Later descendants added a mosque, primary school, cyclone shelter and Eidgah in front; Kutuba union's chairman is a descendant. This is the house whose details (Haider Ali, 1748, three storeys, sal beams, big dighi) the project's first research list attached to the Borhanuddin Chowdhury Bari; the audit wrongly struck them out.
established_era: Zamindari begun in 1155 BS (about 1748 CE) by Haydar Ali, who built the house; Ajker Patrika (2022) calls it 274 years old.
founder_or_family: Zamindar Haydar Ali, said to have held about 4,000 acres and died at 42 after some 20 years as zamindar. Sons Asmat Ali Mia, Hedayet Ali, Ehsan Ali, Emdat Ali, Iakub Ali and Lutfe Ali; Emdad and Lutfe Ali kept the zamindari to 1947, and Iakub Ali was active in the Khilafat and Congress movements (Ajker Patrika, quoting a fifth-generation descendant).
architectural_style: Three-storey main building of lime-surki masonry with 27-inch walls and sal-wood beams that are still sound, four single-storey buildings behind it, and a large dighi on the west; once enclosed by a wide security wall. The estate covers 14 acres 22 decimals (Ajker Patrika).
preservation_status: Dilapidated from lack of upkeep but still attractive; the main building is unoccupied. Descendants maintain the property from a shared fund, and the UNO said in 2022 that steps would be taken to preserve it (Ajker Patrika).

short_description: The seat of the Kirtipasha Sens (Roy Chowdhurys), Baidya zamindars from Porgachha in Bikrampur, about 5 km from Jhalokathi town. Banglapedia says Raja Joynarayan of Selimabad (Rayerkathi) created the Kirtipasha taluk as a reward for the family, who later bought shares of Selimabad pargana itself and took the title Chowdhury after 1793. The estate was split into the ten-anna Boro Hissa and the six-anna Chhoto Hissa, whose feuds historian Tapan Raychaudhuri, born into the Boro Hissa, described in his memoir Bangalnama; he revisited in 2011 or 2012. The family also produced historian Rohini Kumar Roy Chowdhury. Prasanna Kumar Roy Chowdhury founded a school in 1871 and a hospital and library in 1872 (Banglapedia). A sati memorial in the grounds marks the widow of a zamindar who was poisoned; Jugantor (2026) names them Kali Prosanna Kumar and Horosundori Devi and dates the sati to 1828. Today the Boro Hissa natmandir, hall, Durga dalan and pond ghat survive in poor condition amid schools; the district museum opened here in 2004 has closed.
established_era: 18th century for the estate (Banglapedia; Daily Star, 2025); the surviving house is variously dated to the early 19th century (Wikipedia; Jugantor, 2026) or 1900 (Wikipedia infobox).
founder_or_family: Sen (later Roy Chowdhury) family of Bikrampur. Banglapedia names Durgadas Sen as founder of the zamindari; the Daily Star (2025) and Daily Star Bangla (2023) name Krishnakumar Sen, who received the taluk from the Raja of Rayerkathi and split it between his sons Rajaram (10 ana) and Kashiram (6 ana).
architectural_style: Not described in detail; brick and lime mortar with iron rods (Wikipedia).
preservation_status: Main house of the Boro Hissa is ruined: roofs broken, doors and windows stripped, overgrown. Parts are used by schools and a nursing college; the Chhoto Hissa house is gone (Daily Star, Jun 2025; Jugantor, Sep 2026). A conservation proposal sent after a 2017 Department of Archaeology visit was not approved (Daily Star, 2025).

short_description: Locally called Mia Bari, the seat of a Muslim zamindar family at Sreerampur in Dumki upazila, a short ferry and easybike ride from Patuakhali town. The founder, Shib Prasad Mukhopadhyay, served Nawab Murshid Quli Khan, converted to Islam as Shibl Khan and was granted land and the title Mia; his son Kale Khan expanded the zamindari. Surviving pieces include parts of the residential blocks, the Kale Khan Jame Mosque, the joint grave of Kale Khan Mia and his wife Zulekha, a closed 'dark well' and a Mughal-era bridge known as Kale Khan's bridge. Local stories of buried revenue and of tenants thrown into the well are folklore, not documented history.
established_era: 18th century (Mughal period). The zamindari is said to date from the rule of Nawab Murshid Quli Khan (1717-1727); a 2025 Janakantha headline calls the house about 300 years old. English and Bangla Wikipedia infoboxes say '19th century', which contradicts their own text.
founder_or_family: Shibl (Shibal) Khan Mia, born Shib Prasad Mukhopadhyay, a senior official under Nawab Murshid Quli Khan who became a Muslim and received land and the title 'Mia'. His son Kale Khan enlarged the estate to 56 mouzas (Wikipedia; 57 in a Local Guides post).
architectural_style: Mughal-style brick, lime-surki and rod buildings (Wikipedia). The complex had several gates (eight, per a Local Guides post), residential blocks, a 'dark well' (andhakup), a Mughal-style mosque and a Mughal-era bridge over the adjoining canal.
preservation_status: Most structures are close to collapse (Wikipedia, citing NTV 2017 and Protidiner Bangladesh 2023). The gates are gone except for traces; the dark well is closed.

short_description: Seat of the Rayerkathi rajas, zamindars of Selimabad pargana, about 3 km north of Pirojpur town. Khoborsangjog (2022) traces the family to Madan Mohan, revenue collector of Selimabad from 1618, who bought land in his son Srinath's name in 1628; Srinath was made Raja, and his son Rudra Narayan Ray Chowdhury cleared forest near present-day Pirojpur in 1658 and built the palace and a temple, which gave the place its name. The family was the region's senior landholder: Banglapedia says Raja Joynarayan of Selimabad (Rayerkathi) created the Kirtipasha taluk for the Sen family, whose Raghunath Sen became head diwan of Rayerkathi, and the Saturia family's taluk was a reward for helping restore the Rayerkathi zamindari (Wikipedia, Rajapur Upazila). The complex once had a palace, guesthouse, nahabat khana, theatre and temples; the Kali temple with a large Shiva lingam is the best-known survivor.
established_era: Mid-17th century. The Kali temple is dated 1658 (Pirojpur District portal via the audit; Khoborsangjog, 2022); the palace is said to have been built the same year, but only Khoborsangjog says so.
founder_or_family: Rudra Narayan Ray Chowdhury, grandson of Madan Mohan, who collected revenue for Selimabad pargana from 1618; Madan Mohan's son Srinath received the title Raja from a Mughal emperor (Khoborsangjog, 2022). The master list names 'Raja Madan Mohan Rup Narayan', which no source read here supports.
architectural_style: Not described by any source found (palace complex with temples).
preservation_status: Largely ruined. Of about 200 buildings, seven still stand (Khoborsangjog, 2022); the district portal, via the audit, says only a small number remain.

short_description: The estate house of an English landowner in Sapleja union near the Sundarbans, about 50 km from Pirojpur town. Desh Rupantor (May 2026) reports that Edward Parry Casper built it on about 9.25 acres given to him by a local man, Farajullah, and ran the estate through employees Suresh Chandra Sur and Satish Chandra, coming by boat from Barishal each winter to collect rent. A punyaha festival with jatra and folk shows was held at the end of Poush. The local post office, Shilarganj, is said to be named after Casper's father, 'Shilar Saheb'. After Partition the property passed to the government; the upper floor was pulled down and two swords said to have been Casper's are lost. Banglapedia lists it as the 'Kuthibari at Sapleza' and the audit calls it an indigo or planter-era building, but the readable report describes a rent-collecting estate, so it is classed here as a kachari.
established_era: Uncertain: Desh Rupantor (2026) says early 18th century but also calls the building about 200 years old.
founder_or_family: Edward Parry Casper, an Englishman, on land said to have been gifted by a wealthy local man, Farajullah (Desh Rupantor, 2026). The audit reads the Pirojpur District portal as describing land given to an English planter.
architectural_style: British colonial: rectangular main building on 18 arches, once two storeys (Desh Rupantor, 2026).
preservation_status: Abandoned and decaying. The main building lost its upper floor after 1947 and was later used as the union land (tahsil) office until a new office was built beside it; three buildings need urgent repair. A Department of Archaeology official said a preservation proposal had been sent, without knowing whether it was gazetted (Desh Rupantor, May 2026).

short_description: The ruins of the last residence of the Bakla-Chandradwip rajas, spread over about 30 acres at Madhabpasha beside the Barishal–Banaripara road. Chandradwip was founded in the early 14th century by Danujamardana Deva after he was driven from Sonargaon; its capital was at Kachua in present Bauphal until Kandarpa Narayan, one of the Baro Bhuiyan, moved it to Madhabpasha to escape Magh raids. In 1611 Raja Ramchandra surrendered to the Mughals and the kingdom became a zamindari. A brass cannon five cubits long inscribed with Kandarpa Narayan's name was found here; Raja Uday Narayan's 18th-century samadhi temple stands 183 m away and a Shiva temple of the period a few hundred metres east.
established_era: Capital moved here from Kachua under Kandarpa Narayan (late 16th century)
founder_or_family: Chandradwip rajas: Danujamardana Deva (founder), Ramaballabh, Krishnaballabh, Hariballabh, Joydev, Kamala Sundari; later the Basu line and Kandarpa Narayan
architectural_style: Overgrown brick ruins; an 18th-century samadhi temple of Raja Uday Narayan on a 6 ft platform 183 m away, with carved deities
preservation_status: Ruins on about 30 acres (the book, 2024)

alternate_names: Gokarna Nawab Bari Complex; Nawab Sir Syed Shamsul Huda Complex; নবাব স্যার সৈয়দ শামসুল হুদা কমপ্লেক্স

The complex includes the two-storey Nawab bari and a mosque. In 1915 he founded a school on the family's ancestral land, now Gokarna Syed Waliullah High School and College. This is a nawab's family seat rather than a documented zamindari palace; no source read describes the house's condition.

short_description: A three-storey riverfront palace on about five acres on the east bank of the Titas, built in the 1840s by the Roy Chowdhury zamindars Gauri Prasad and Krishna Prasad. It has about 60 rooms, including a durbar hall, music and dance halls and a treasury, plus temples and a bathing ghat on the river side. The family left for Kolkata after 1947 and the house came under the Vested Property Act; priests and descendants lived in it until the district administration moved them out in 2023. It is a well-known film location (Madhumalati, Nairabi, Ghetuputra Komola).

founder_or_family: Zamindars Gauri Prasad Roy Chowdhury and Krishna Prasad Roy Chowdhury
architectural_style: Three-storey brick-and-lime (surki) palace built without iron rods; The Daily Star calls it Mughal-style
preservation_status: Declared an archaeological site in 2018. Badly deteriorated; Department of Archaeology restoration under way since 2016. Families living there were moved out in 2023.

short_description: The Basu zamindars' house at Koraitoli bazar, locally called Babur Bari. Harish Chandra Basu of Barishal bought the estate at auction in BS 1220 and ran it for about 70 years. The family left for North 24 Parganas in 1948, and the estate ended in 1951 under Govinda Basu. The site had a three-storey residence, two two-storey blocks, a Durga temple, the large Babur Dighi with a stone ghat, a darbar hall, a tunnel (later filled with sand) and a vault locals call Andhar Manik. It is now an abandoned, overgrown ruin.

A Somewhere in Blog author argues the math is really a memorial pillar. The house is dilapidated; the math was renovated in 2024.

The estate has three brick buildings (a main house, one beside it and one behind), a kachari ghar, the Masjid-e-Noor mosque, the family graveyard, a ghat-lined pond, an entrance gate and a large open field. The family is remembered for helping freedom fighters in 1971. Khan Bahadur Abidur Reza Chowdhury, a British-era politician, belonged to it.

short_description: Seat of the Roy family of Jahapur on the Gomti in Muradnagar. The family were jute traders before buying the zamindari in 1862 (BSS says from the Nawabs of Dhaka; Vromon Guide names Radhika Mohan Das). The roughly 3-acre complex has ten buildings, one of three storeys and nine of two, a lion gate, a Jagannath temple and chariot house added by Ashwini Kumar Roy (1324 BS), elephant and horse stables and a large pond with a ghat. The family still keeps original furniture and holds periodic pujas.
established_era: Zamindari acquired in 1862 (BSS 2023, Bangla Wikipedia, Vromon Guide); the family is said to have lived in Jahapur for about 400 years.
founder_or_family: Gouri Mohan Roy (seventh generation of a line begun by Kanai Lal Roy), with his brothers Ram Dayal and Kamala Kanta, per BSS 2023 and Bangla Wikipedia. The master list's 'Ramkamal Roy' appears in no other source.
architectural_style: Brick-and-surkhi buildings laid out in I and L shapes, with floral plasterwork, decorative window grilles and wide verandas; Bangla Wikipedia calls the designs Mughal-influenced and says craftsmen were brought from Bikrampur.
preservation_status: Unprotected and still lived in by descendants (11th generation per Bangla Wikipedia). BSS (June 2023) says most buildings are dilapidated and overgrown, two are destroyed and one of the gate lions has collapsed; the Department of Archaeology said it would inspect the site.

short_description: Roy family estate in Titas whose zamindari spread over Meghna, Titas, Homna and Muradnagar. Family members included Khetra Mohan Roy, the area's first graduate and lawyer, and Upendra Chandra Roy, its first graduate doctor. The family left for India after Partition and no heirs have been traced. The site has 13 surviving buildings, a large dighi, about 20 ponds and reported tunnels. preservation_status: Unprotected and badly decayed. Of 17 buildings, 4 were demolished by locals; the rest are moss-covered and some are occupied by local groups, with one resident alleging seizure through fake documents (Dhaka Tribune 2017). The dighi and ponds survive.

The zamindari ended in 1950, but family members stayed until attacks and looting around the late 1990s, then moved to Dhaka, Chattogram, Tripura and Kolkata. Hindu devotees hold a fair at the house every Baishakh. The founder's name and the building date differ widely between sources.

short_description: Seat of the Mong Circle chiefs (Mong rajas), one of the three hereditary chieftaincies of the Chittagong Hill Tracts. It is a circle chief's seat, not an ordinary Bengal zamindar estate: the raja oversees jhum-tax collection through mouza headmen and village karbaris, under a system the British formalised in the CHT Regulation of 1900. In 1971 Raja Mong Prue Sein sheltered people fleeing Chattogram here, turned the hall into a temporary hospital where Rani Nihar Devi worked as a midwife, and gave weapons and vehicles to the Mukti Bahini.
established_era: Mong Circle dates to 1782 (Wikipedia); the Manikchhari rajbari was founded in 1861 (Prothom Alo, 2024)

architectural_style: Not documented as a style. About 5 acres holding a single-storey main building, a semi-pucca kachari, the carved Nanuma Debi Hall and a Buddhist vihara.
preservation_status: Family property, quiet and little used. The Nanuma Debi Hall was renovated after falling into ruin; the pond is dry. Visitors need the family's permission; Mejo Kumar Suichingpru looks after upkeep (Prothom Alo, Dec 2024).

preservation_status: In ruins. Walls overgrown, interior littered (Prothom Alo, Nov 2024). A boundary wall was built in 2021 under the Department of Archaeology, with the district administration running the project.

A fire of unknown cause destroyed the later palace in November 2010, taking with it a chair used by Rani Kalindi and papers on the Raj Punnah.

His sons Tushar Pal and Tridib Pal sold the property and left for India; the main house is abandoned and overgrown.

short_description: The riverside palace of the Nawabs of Dhaka, the largest Muslim zamindar family of East Bengal, built between 1859 and 1872 by Nawab Abdul Ghani and named after his son Ahsanullah. After decades of decay it was restored and opened as a museum in 1992, with its pink facade and lotus-bud dome now one of Dhaka's best-known landmarks.

The government bought it in 2018 for about Tk 331.7 crore, and after restoration the Department of Archaeology opened it to visitors in 2025.

short_description: A riverfront mansion in Farashganj that began as Armenian merchant Stephen Aratoon's house (1825) and was bought in 1840 by the merchant brothers Ruplal and Raghunath Das, who had it rebuilt to a Calcutta Martin and Company design. In 1888 it hosted a ball for Viceroy Lord Dufferin, beating Ahsan Manzil for the honour, and it was a centre of classical music. After the family left in 1947 it was split among occupants and claimants; today its ground floor is part of Dhaka's largest spice market and the building is badly decayed.

short_description: A riverside compound at Dewanbari village in Aminbazar, Savar, just past the Gabtoli bridge on the north-west edge of Dhaka. Md. Mahmud Ali's book says it was built around 1810-1815 for a dewan (chief revenue official) and later bought by Janab Ali, a trader and Savar's first Haji, which is why it is also called Haji Bari. The Daily Star and Dhaka Tribune both credit Janab Ali with building it in 1880. The compound has a two-storey main house, residential blocks around courtyards, a pond with ghats, a family graveyard and a three-domed chini-tikri mosque. It was gazetted as a heritage site in 2009, but owners and architects say nothing has been done to conserve it.
established_era: Disputed: c. 1810-1815 as a dewan's house (Purbo Bongger Jomidar Bari) vs built 1880 by Haji Janab Ali (The Daily Star 2019; Dhaka Tribune 2019, for the mosque). Upper floor added in the Pakistan period (book).
founder_or_family: Disputed: an unnamed dewan (revenue official), with Janab Ali buying it about 150 years ago (book); or Alhaj Janab Ali himself, called a revenue collector of the East India Company (Daily Star) or a wholesale leather trader (Dhaka Tribune)
architectural_style: Colonial-era residential compound with a three-domed oblong mosque decorated in chini-tikri (broken-china mosaic)
preservation_status: Listed heritage site (government gazette, 2 February 2009) but unconserved. Only the main house is liveable; the east block is almost in ruins, the boundary wall half-demolished and much of the pond filled for a road (The Daily Star, 2019). Owned by about 50 descendants of Janab Ali.

name_en: Khalia Zamindar Bari (Rajaram Roy Chowdhury's Estate)
alternate_names: Rajaram Roy's house; রাজারাম রায়ের বাড়ি; Raja Rammohan Roy Chowdhury's zamindari (Bangla Wikipedia infobox); Rajaram Mandir; রাজারাম মন্দির
coordinates_note: No coordinates found. Khalia village, about 10 minutes by van from Tekerhat bus stand on the Dhaka-Khulna highway (MyTourBD).
short_description: Khalia was one of seven estates of the Ujani zamindars; tradition says it was given to Rajaram Roy after the zamindar's wife saw an auspicious birthmark on him. Rajaram built a 250-acre seat with houses, a garden house, a puja mandap and a terracotta temple, and founded the Rajaram Institute school. The temple is a protected monument while the houses are crumbling.
established_era: 18th century zamindari (Bangla Wikipedia: c. 1700s); Rajaram temple dated 17th century (Madaripur district portal) or 1825 (MyTourBD)
founder_or_family: Rajaram Roy Chowdhury, who by local tradition received Khalia as a gift from the Ujani zamindars
architectural_style: Two- and three-storey brick-and-surki buildings; two-storey terracotta temple
preservation_status: Residential buildings near collapse from neglect; the Rajaram temple is protected by the Department of Archaeology and in fair condition.

Six small maths, four paved ponds and a cremation ghat surround them. The Saha family left for Kolkata during the 1971 war, and the site, now called Howlader Bari after its buyer, is mostly in ruins.

Four front blocks with lion-topped gates, inner quarters behind and a pond with bathing ghats make it one of the best-preserved zamindar palaces in Bangladesh. The central Rang Mahal is now a museum run by the Department of Archaeology.

alternate_names: বেতিলা জমিদারবাড়ি; Satu Babu's house; সত্য বাবুর বাড়ি; Betila Palace
coordinates_note: TouristPlaces/OpenStreetMap (23.83741, 90.02448) and Adar Bepari (23.837466, 90.024462) agree within about 10 m; both may come from the same map pin. Near Betila bazar.
short_description: Locally called a zamindar bari, Betila was really the home of a family of Kolkata jute traders who settled here because the Betila canal (the Nurani river) linked the Dhaleshwari and Kaliganga and was a safe route for cargo boats. Local accounts name Jyotindra Saha ('Jyoti Babu') as the ancestor and Satyendra Kumar Chowdhury ('Satya Babu'), son of Harendra Kumar Chowdhury, as its best-known owner. Written records are scarce. The Department of Social Services leased it from the Ministry of Land as a shelter home, but by 2021 it had no residents, the Public Works Department had declared both buildings abandoned, and the plaster, doors, ghats and boundary walls were decaying.
established_era: British colonial period; no construction date recorded
founder_or_family: Jyotindra Saha (Jyotindra Kumar Chowdhury, 'Jyoti Babu'), a Kolkata jute merchant, per local accounts; later home of Satyendra Kumar Chowdhury (Saha), 'Satya Babu'
architectural_style: Two matching two-storey colonial-era buildings of lime, brick-and-stone and iron
preservation_status: Standing but neglected; used as a government shelter home, closed by 2021 and declared abandoned (unsafe) by the Public Works Department

short_description: Founded by Narasingha Roy Chowdhury, whose family came from Delhi. The line ran through Girishgobinda Roy Chowdhury to Hemchandra Roy Chowdhury and his three sons, Amulyachandra, Birendrachandra and Nirmalchandra; locals still call it Hemchandra's house. The estate ran 24 kacharis and held land as far as Jagannathpur and Khaliajuri in greater Mymensingh. Hemchandra founded a school beside the house in 1917, named after his father. After the zamindari system ended the family left for India (1952 per Wikipedia). A 2025 visitor found the lion gateway, turrets, reception hall and colourful room floors weathered and largely abandoned.
established_era: Unknown (British colonial zamindari era); school beside the house founded in 1917

preservation_status: Standing but dilapidated (Halfashion, 2025); Bangla Wikipedia and Adar Bepari say part is used as a government land office

established_era: Founded late 18th century; surviving buildings early 19th to early 20th century
founder_or_family: Panchanan Sen / Panchanan Chaudhuri (Dasgupta family, b. c.1740), tobacco trader in Dinajpur; later held by the Joy Sankar and Hem Sankar branches
architectural_style: Mughal-European hybrid; Navaratna (nine-spired) temple
preservation_status: In ruins: abandoned since 1947-57, encroached; Department of Archaeology signboards but no restoration of the palace

alternate_names: Bailyapara Zamindar Bari (local); বাইল্যাপাড়া জমিদার বাড়ি; Mukunda Murari's house; মুকুন্দ মুরারির বাড়ি
coordinates_note: GPS 23°46'13.7"N 90°35'16.0"E from a visitor's photo log (somewhereinblog, qshohenq, Sep 2022), just north of Baliapara's main road. The same author logged a second old building ('Baliapara Zamindar Bari - 2') at 23°46'11.7"N 90°35'14.5"E, about 65 m away. Not cross-checked against a map service (unreachable from this session).
short_description: An L-shaped, three-storey red-brick house built around the 1900s by Mukunda Murari, a treasurer-turned-trader who bought a zamindari. He left for India after Partition but kept the house because a daughter had married in Narayanganj, and in 1966 leased it to a local school committee. Today it stands empty, overgrown and partly collapsed.
established_era: Early 20th century (about 1900s; roughly 100+ years old per visitor accounts)
founder_or_family: Mukunda Murari (also written Murali), a former khajanchi (treasurer) of zamindar Kishori Poddar who prospered in trade in Dhaka and Narayanganj and later bought a zamindari
architectural_style: Colonial-era vernacular: red brick in lime-surki mortar, L-shaped three-storey plan
preservation_status: In ruins: unprotected; roof of the upper left section collapsed after an earthquake; overgrown

alternate_names: Baro Sardar Bari; Bara Sardarbari; বড় সর্দার বাড়ি; Isha Khan Bari / Isha Khar Zamindar Bari (popular name, not supported by sources); ঈশা খাঁ বাড়ি / ঈসা খাঁ জমিদার বাড়ি (লোকমুখে প্রচলিত); Chhoto Sardar Bari (name reportedly used on Bangla Wikipedia)
locality: Sonargaon (inside the Bangladesh Folk Art and Crafts Foundation complex, near Panam Nagar)
locality_bn: সোনারগাঁও (বাংলাদেশ লোক ও কারুশিল্প ফাউন্ডেশন চত্বর, পানাম নগরের কাছে)
coordinates_note: GPS 23°38'57.2"N 90°36'01.0"E from a visitor's photo log (somewhereinblog, qshohenq, Mar 2023). Consistent with the house's position inside the Folk Art Museum grounds near Panam Nagar; Wikipedia and map services could not be reached from this research session to cross-check. Confirm on Google Maps before publishing.
short_description: A two-storey, 85-room mansion around two courtyards, flanked by east and west ponds, inside the Bangladesh Folk Art and Crafts Foundation at Sonargaon. Conservation research found it grew in about six phases, from a much older core to a 1902 colonial front, rather than being a single zamindar palace. Restored to its original look between 2012 and 2016 with Korean funding, it now displays folk crafts and won the IAB Award in 2023.
established_era: Multi-phase: an early core possibly pre-Mughal or early Mughal (per conservation research); main front block dated by inscription to 1902 (1308 BS), with further additions in 1904 and c. 1923 (1330 BS)
founder_or_family: Uncertain. A local merchant family of the Saha 'Sardar' clan is usually credited (one visitor account names Gopinath Saha Sardar or Aishwaryakanta Saha Sardar; unverified). The popular attribution to Isa Khan is a legend.
architectural_style: Colonial-era front (arched verandas, cast-iron railings, chini-tikri mosaic gatehouse) wrapped around older Mughal-period brick blocks; lime-surki masonry
preservation_status: Preserved: government-owned (acquired 1972), restored 2012-2016 with funding from South Korea's Youngone Corporation; now part of the Sonargaon Folk Art and Crafts Museum

name_en: Gopaldi Zamindar Bari (Sadasadi Zamindar Bari / Bhuiyan Bari)
alternate_names: Sadasadi Zamindar Bari; Sodasodi Zamindar Palace; সদাসদী জমিদার বাড়ি; Bhuiyan Bari; ভূঁইয়া বাড়ি / ভূঁঞা বাড়ি; 101-room zamindar house; ১০১ কক্ষের জমিদার বাড়ি; Sadasardi 108-room two-storey building (Banglapedia); ১০৮ কক্ষ বিশিষ্ট দ্বিতল ভবন (সাদাসর্দি)
union: Gopaldi Pourashava (municipality); Banglapedia lists the building under Sadasardi
coordinates_note: Pin from Google Maps given by the project editor on 13 Oct 2026; it sits in Sadasadi, about 6-7 km east of Araihazar town as travel guides describe. Not yet cross-checked against a second source.
short_description: A large two-storey mansion of about 101 rooms (Banglapedia says 108) built around a courtyard in Sadasadi, Gopaldi, by the Bhuiyan zamindar family, one of three zamindar families (Sardar, Teli and Bhuiyan) of Gopaldi. Carved verandah pillars, carved doors in every room and a pond with separate ghats for men and women survive. The house is badly decayed: walls have fallen, plaster is peeling, the kitchen has collapsed and fittings have been stolen.
established_era: Early 20th century: built 1323 BS (about 1916-17) per travel guides; the area's zamindar families date back about 150 years
founder_or_family: Bhuiyan family of Gopaldi: brothers Harichandra (Harichand) and Ramkanai Bhuiyan; later held by son-in-law Rishikaj Babu and last zamindar Jagabandhu Babu, whose wife Binodini Saha managed the estate
architectural_style: Colonial-era two-storey courtyard mansion with carved pillars, doors and windows; one blogger notes Mughal influence
preservation_status: In ruins: unprotected and neglected, with collapsed walls and stolen fittings

alternate_names: Murapara Palace; মুড়াপাড়া রাজবাড়ি; Murapara Degree College campus
coordinates_note: From English Wikipedia only; consistent with '~25 km SE of Dhaka, 5 km off the Dhaka-Sylhet road'. Confirm on Google Maps before publishing.
short_description: A two-storey palace with a 200-foot west-facing front, built in stages between 1889 and 1909 by the Banerjee family, whose founder had served the Natore Raj. Its verandah arches are filled with cast-iron tracery and coloured glass. Abandoned after 1947, it has housed a school and college since 1966, which has kept it in better shape than most.
established_era: Late 19th - early 20th century (built 1889-1909)
founder_or_family: Ramratan Banerjee, treasurer of the Natore Raj; palace begun by his descendant Pratap Chandra Banerjee in 1889
architectural_style: Colonial Neoclassical with Indo-Saracenic and Bengali elements (Corinthian columns, pediment, chauchala-domed pinnacles, coloured-glass arches)
preservation_status: Good condition; adaptive reuse as Murapara Degree College (since 1966); government property since 1948

alternate_names: Yogesh/Jogesh Babur Bari; যোগেশ বাবুর বাড়ি; Babur Bari; বাবুর বাড়ি; Monorama Bash (local); মনোরমা বাস
coordinates_note: Pin from Google Maps given by the project editor on 13 Oct 2026; it sits in Satgram near Purinda bus stand on the Dhaka-Sylhet highway. Not yet cross-checked against a second source.
short_description: A ruined colonial-era brick mansion in Satgram, Araihazar, locally called Babur Bari or Monorama Bash and linked to Jogesh Gupta, son of Dhaka civic figure Sarat Gupta. The family left for Kolkata after 1947; the house later served as a school and, in 1971, as a freedom fighters' camp. A pond with a stone-paved ghat and remnants of a flower garden survive beside the crumbling house.
established_era: British colonial period (exact year unknown; locally said to be early in British rule)
founder_or_family: Unconfirmed builder; associated with Jogesh (Yogesh) Gupta, eldest son of Sarat Gupta, a deputy mayor of Dhaka in British times after whom Sarat Gupta Road, Lakshmibazar, is named (Risingbd)
architectural_style: Colonial-era brick mansion (at least two storeys) with ornamental cast-iron veranda railings
preservation_status: In ruins: unprotected; broken walls with roots, moss and plants in the brickwork

name_en: Balapur Zamindar Bari (Nabin Chandra Saha Zamindar Bari)
name_bn: বালাপুর জমিদার বাড়ি (নবীন চন্দ্র সাহার জমিদার বাড়ি)
alternate_names: Balapur Jamidar Bari; নবীন চন্দ্র সাহা জমিদার বাড়ি; Kali Babu's house (after zamindar Kali Mohan Saha); বালাপুর জমিদার বাড়ী
coordinates_note: From Adar Bepari's Google Maps link, which is labelled 'Balapur high school playground' (23.8337529, 90.7001806). Balapur Nabin Chandra High School adjoins the palace (RisingBD 2019; Daily Star 2016), so the house should be within a few hundred metres. No second independent coordinate found; confirm the exact building on a map before publishing.
short_description: A 103-room Saha family palace on the bank of the Meghna, founded by zamindar Nabin Chandra Saha on a roughly 320-bigha estate. Wings of one, two and three storeys enclose the compound, with mosaic floors, carved doors, a 31-room guest block, ponds with stone ghats, a Durga mandap and temples. The family left for Kolkata in 1947; since then the house has decayed, and in 2019 signboards declared it dangerous.
established_era: Mid-to-late 19th century (described as ~150 years old in 2019); exact date unknown
founder_or_family: Nabin Chandra Saha; the leading zamindar was Kali Mohan Saha ('Kali Babu')
architectural_style: Colonial-era Bengali zamindar palace: multi-wing courtyard plan, mosaic/tile floors, floral-carved doors and windows
preservation_status: In ruins: abandoned and unprotected; declared dangerous with no-entry signboards (2019); residents moved out in 2013; temple ruined; property claimed by various parties

name_en: Ghorashal Zamindar Bari (Monu Mia's Zamindar Bari)
name_bn: ঘোড়াশাল জমিদার বাড়ি (মনু মিয়ার জমিদার বাড়ি)
alternate_names: Monu Mia Zamindar House; Manu Miah's House; মনু মিয়ার বাড়ি; ঘোড়াশাল মিঞা বাড়ি; Ghorashal Mia Bari
coordinates_note: Adar Bepari's Google Maps link (23.9366853, 90.6224294) and Offroad Bangladesh's map pin (23.9361, 90.6216) agree within ~110 m. Both sit about 400 m south of Wikipedia's Ghorashal town centre (23.940, 90.622) and near Ghorashal bus stand, as the travel sources describe.
short_description: A compound of three white mansions on about 10 acres in Ghorashal, belonging to the Muslim zamindar family whose best-known son was Ahmadul Kabir 'Monu Mia' (1923-2003), editor of the daily Sangbad and an MP. Unlike most zamindar houses in the area it has been kept up, with Corinthian-columned facades, a mosque at the gate, paved ponds and gardens. It is still private property, so visitors walk the grounds with permission.
established_era: First building said to date from 1176 BS (~1769-70 CE); main house reconstructed 1335 BS (~1928-29 CE). Family roots traced to the Mughal period.
founder_or_family: Disputed: the Muslim zamindar family of Ghorashal, variously traced to Sheikh Golam Nabi (Mughal period) or to Abu Yusuf Lutful Kabir 'Fenu Mia'; a 'Sazda/Sajda Mia' is credited with the 1335 BS rebuild
architectural_style: Colonial Classical (Corinthian columns, arched doorways, leaf-motif parapet), white-washed
preservation_status: Well maintained private family property, still in the zamindar family's hands; not a protected monument. Grounds visitable with permission.

name_en: Lakshman Saha Zamindar Bari (Danga Zamindar Bari)
name_bn: লক্ষণ সাহার জমিদার বাড়ি (ডাঙ্গা জমিদার বাড়ি)
alternate_names: Lokkhon Saha Zamindar Bari; Lakshan Saha's Zamindar House; Ukil Bari / Ukiler Bari (the lawyer's house); উকিল বাড়ি; Jamina Mahal (name given by the later owner); ডাংগা জমিদার বাড়ি
coordinates_note: Bangla Wikipedia infobox (23°53'56.82"N 90°35'41.48"E = 23.89912, 90.59486) and Adar Bepari's Google Maps link (23.8990967, 90.5948446) agree within a few metres. They may share an origin (a Google Maps pin), but both match the guides' description of the house about 1 km from Danga Bazar.
short_description: A two-storey carved house built by Lakshman Saha, a Hindu sub-zamindar of Danga, beside a pond with a black-stone (kashti) ghat and the remains of the temples that once ringed it. After his sons left for India, a grandson sold it to lawyer Ahmed Ali, which is why locals call it the Ukil Bari. It is the most ornate of several Saha houses in Danga and still stands, though unprotected.
established_era: Uncertain: Bangla Wikipedia gives 19th century; Daily Janakantha (2025) calls Lakshman Saha a Mughal-era zamindar and the house 'a century old'
founder_or_family: Lakshman (Lakkhan) Saha, a sub-zamindar under a larger zamindar
architectural_style: Colonial with Mughal elements (Bangla Wikipedia); ornate carved two-storey house with flat roof
preservation_status: Not protected; private property of the Ahmed Ali (lawyer) family. Main house standing in fair condition; pond temples mostly collapsed. Locals and the union parishad have asked for conservation (2025); ownership is disputed in court.

alternate_names: Loxmikol Raja Bari; Laxmikol Rajbari; Raja Surya Kumar's palace; রাজা সূর্য কুমারের বাড়ি; লক্ষ্মীকোল রাজবাড়ি
coordinates_note: GeoNames centre of Lakshmikol village, not the palace site. Pin 'Collectorate Dighi / Alla Newaj Khairu Academy, Lakshmikol' by hand before publishing.
short_description: Seat of Raja Surya Kumar Guha Roy, who received the title Raja in 1885 for public works and founded the Raja Surya Kumar Institution in 1888. The roughly 60-acre complex had a guest house, kachari, tol, stables and a stone-paved pond. Nothing of the palace survives; one tradition says the district takes its name from this 'Rajbari'.
established_era: 18th-19th century seat of the Guha Roy family; Surya Kumar made Raja in 1885
founder_or_family: Guha Roy family (ancestor Prabhuram, who served Nawab Siraj-ud-Daulah); best known as the seat of Raja Surya Kumar Guha Roy (d. c.1912)
architectural_style: Not recorded; palace no longer exists
preservation_status: Lost: palace demolished. Only Collectorate Dighi, an old banyan tree and a pond ghat remain; a school stands on the site.

alternate_names: Pachuria Zamindar Bari; পাচুরিয়া জমিদার বাড়ি; Panchuria zamindar houses; Peshkar Bari; পেশকার বাড়ি; unverified); unverified)

short_description: A cluster of at least four zamindar houses in Panchuria union, three of them close together near Peshkar Mor beside the railway. The biggest became Peshkar Bari after a court clerk bought it in the 1950s; another belonged to Bonomali Saha. All are now private homes. The book describes Kuthi Pachuria, Kholabaria and Mukundia in this union as separate houses (their own records); whether any of them is among the houses here is not known.
established_era: Unknown; owners left after 1947 and Peshkar Bari was sold in the 1950s
founder_or_family: Several zamindar families; only Bonomali Saha ('the smallest of the zamindars') is named. The largest house's owner is forgotten.
architectural_style: Not described; 'old and majestic' houses (TBS)
preservation_status: Private homes: Peshkar Bari standing and lived in; the Saha house about half destroyed. Not protected.

coordinates_note: No coordinates found. Haturia, Gosairhat upazila, a former steamer station (Travel News Bangladesh).
short_description: Haturia in Gosairhat was a steamer station and the home of the British-era Muslim zamindars Sekander Ali Chowdhury and Roshan Ali Chowdhury. Kalikrishna Thakur of the Kolkata Thakur family also kept an estate office here, which reportedly survives. No description of the zamindar house itself was found.
established_era: British period
founder_or_family: Muslim Chowdhury zamindars: Sekander Ali Chowdhury and his son Roshan Ali Chowdhury; Nawab Ali Chowdhury is also named. The Kolkata Thakur family's zamindar Kalikrishna Thakur kept a kachari (estate office) here.
architectural_style: Not documented
preservation_status: Not documented; the Thakur family's kachari is said to still stand

alternate_names: Kartikpur Chowdhury Bari; কার্তিকপুর চৌধুরী বাড়ি
coordinates_note: Adar Bepari map pin (23.25228, 90.4754903). Not cross-checked. The gate is about 80 m off the Naria-Bhedarganj road; part of Kartikpur village falls in Ramvadrapur union of Bhedarganj upazila (Adar Bepari).
short_description: The seat of the Chowdhury zamindars of Kartikpur, who trace their line to a Mughal commander who settled here after Kedar Roy's defeat. A richly ornamented two-storey house, a gate with an illegible inscription and a row of small decorative minarets survive. The village name is said to come from Kartik Sen, a grandson of Lakshman Sen, who sheltered here after Bakhtiyar Khilji's conquest.
established_era: Zamindari about 200 years old; the house is called about 400 years old in the same source (unverified, likely 19th century)
founder_or_family: Chowdhury family descended from Fateh Muhammad, a Mughal commander who married the daughter of Sheikh Kalu, a commander of Kedar Roy (family tradition reported by Adar Bepari)
architectural_style: Ornate two-storey colonial-era brick house with a decorated gateway and small minarets along the approach
preservation_status: Abandoned and propped with iron sheets against collapse; a high school stands on the former pond ghat. Climbing to the roof is forbidden. No protected status found.

name_en: Rudrakar Zamindar Bari and Math (Babu Bari)
alternate_names: Rudrakar Math; রুদ্রকর মঠ; Babu Bari Math; বাবু বাড়ি মঠ; Rudrakar Moth
coordinates_note: Adar Bepari map pin for the math (23.1830312, 90.3458762). Consistent with Dhaka Tribune (about 3 km south of the DC office) and Vromonkari (about 5 km south-east of town, near Rudrakar Union Parishad on the Shariatpur-Damudya road), but those give no coordinates.
short_description: The Chakraborty zamindars of Rudrakar built a memorial math, about 20 m tall with four corner turrets and goddess figures on its third tier, beside a large pond and their multi-storey residences. Nilmoni Chakraborty founded the Rudrakar Nilmoni High School in 1925. The math survived shelling in 1971, but after the last zamindar's family left the complex decayed and was occupied.
established_era: Late 19th to early 20th century: gate inscription records a renovation in 1296 BS (c. 1889); the math is said to have been rebuilt in 1898; one source dates the math to 1305-1315 BS (c. 1898-1908)
founder_or_family: Chakraborty zamindars of Rudrakar: Nilmoni Chakraborty and his sons Banilal, Khitilal and Boshontolal (Dhaka Tribune), or zamindar Gurucharan Chakraborty (Adar Bepari, MyTourBD)
architectural_style: Tall pancharatna-style memorial math (central tower with four corner turrets) with plaster carvings, beside multi-storey colonial-era residences
preservation_status: Ruined and occupied: of 8-10 original buildings, three survive (two three-storey, one ground floor only), partly held by occupiers; the math's plaster is falling. District officials have asked the Department of Archaeology to restore it; not yet protected.

alternate_names: Alisha Kanda Roy Bari; আলীশাকান্দা রায়বাড়ি
coordinates_note: No coordinates or upazila confirmed. Techzoom (2021) says it is reached by CNG from Tangail Sadar, or by auto via Binnafoir bazar or Charabari. Pin it on a map before publishing.

Descendants still live upstairs and have said they would donate it for restoration or public use. Only one published source describes it, so details need checking on the ground.
established_era: Unknown (late zamindari era)
founder_or_family: Zamindar Upendra Sen (Techzoom 2021, single source)
architectural_style: Two-storey brick house built with bricks fired by the family
preservation_status: Standing; descendants live on the upper floor and the rest is mostly empty

alternate_names: Aloya Zamindar Bari; অলোয়া জমিদার বাড়ি; Aloa Bhabani Rajbari
coordinates_note: No published coordinates found. Bangla Wikipedia places it inside Tangail municipality; a 2019 blog says it is a short auto ride from Santosh. Pin it on a map before publishing.
short_description: A small Hindu zamindar house on 132 decimals of land on the edge of Tangail town. The last zamindar, Konok Lota Roy Chowdhury, left for India with the family in 1950. Since 1980 a corner of the building has housed a government land office, while the rest is decaying and largely unused.
founder_or_family: Sachi Nath Roy Chowdhury, who reportedly moved from Mymensingh
architectural_style: Colonial-era brick, lime-surki and iron-rod mansion with decorative cement work
preservation_status: In ruins: one room serves as the union land office (since 1980); the rest is abandoned

founder_or_family: Zamindar Charu Chandra Roy
architectural_style: Brick house with painted interior walls
preservation_status: Unknown

name_en: Delduar Zamindar Bari (North House / Uttar Taraf)
alternate_names: North House; নর্থ হাউস; Uttar Taraf; উত্তর তরফ; Ghaznavi Bari
coordinates_note: No published coordinates found. It is in Delduar town; a 2019 visitor needed a rickshaw driver to find it.
short_description: Home of the Ghaznavis, one of Tangail's few Muslim zamindar families. Sir Abdul Karim Ghaznavi and Sir Abdul Halim Ghaznavi were ministers and businessmen in British Bengal, and their mother Karimunnesa Khanam Chowdhurani was Begum Rokeya's sister. The novelist Mir Mosharraf Hossain served as the estate's manager from 1885. The walled single-storey house, family graveyard and mosque are maintained, but visitors need a caretaker's permission.
established_era: Unknown; family prominent from the 19th century (Abdul Karim Ghaznavi took charge in 1894)
founder_or_family: Fatehdad Khan Ghaznavi Lohani (Ghaznavi family of Afghan descent)
architectural_style: Single-storey colonial-style house (Bangla Wikipedia); Rising BD describes Mughal-style elements
preservation_status: Well kept private residence of the Ghaznavi descendants with a caretaker; entry restricted

alternate_names: Dhalapara Chowdhury Bari; ধলাপাড়া চৌধুরীবাড়ী
coordinates_note: No published coordinates found. About 12 km east of Ghatail Sadar near the Bangshai river, beside Dhalapara bazar (mytourbd).
short_description: The Chowdhurys of Dhalapara began in a thatched house in 1223 BS, moved to tin and then built a brick mansion on 7-8 acres. Their best-known member, Amir Ali Chowdhury, was a lawyer and in 1951 the second Muslim chairman of Tangail municipality. The family's Dhalapara Central Mosque (1323 BS) stands north of the bazar.
established_era: 1223 BS (c. 1816); brick mansion about a century old
founder_or_family: The Chowdhury family, said to descend from Shah Ekin
architectural_style: Brick mansion with an octagonal (atchala) kachari house

short_description: This is not a Bengali zamindar's palace but the estate house of the Morrels, British indigo planters after whom Morrelganj is named. In 1849 the family leased forest land at the mouth of the Baleshwar, brought labourers from Barishal and founded a bazaar that became Morrelganj and, for a time, a river port. The estate included a mansion, warehouse, a lock-up and quarters for armed retainers (lathials). In November 1861 the Morrels' men raided the house of the peasant leader Rahimullah of Baraikhali, who was killed, an episode remembered as part of the indigo resistance. The family's hold on the area ended in 1878. Protidiner Sangbad describes a stable reached by a hidden stair, a dance hall, a store and a punishment room, all now decaying.
founder_or_family: The Morrel family, British indigo planters: the widow of a Mr. Morrel and her sons Robert and Henry Morrel, who took a lease of Sundarbans forest land at the mouth of the Baleshwar (Panguchi) river in 1849. Henry Morrel ran the indigo factory.
architectural_style: Colonial planter's house (not described in detail)
preservation_status: Ruinous and abandoned. Protidiner Sangbad (Feb 2023) reports the building collapsing, its doors, windows, grilles, safes and stairs stolen, and land encroached; a memorial pillar to Robert Morrel nearby has also been stripped.

short_description: Colonial-era zamindar house in Kashipur village, KDK union, Jibannagar, about 7 km from the upazila town beside the Bhairab river. Before 1947 the area was in Nadia district. Locals say it was built in 1861 and that the zamindar (Binoy Kumar Majumdar, or the brothers Minay and Vinay Kumar) exchanged about 1,200 bighas with the present residents' ancestors and left for India. The house still holds the zamindars' sofas, beds, tables and a water-lifting motor, with a granary and a well; a krishnachura and a banyan stand at the gate. Local reports tie it to Sarat Chandra Chattopadhyay's story 'Mahesh', saying he was the zamindar's nephew and wrote it after seeing tenants mistreated here; no literary-history source confirms this.
established_era: 1861 according to local residents (Somoy BD, English Wikipedia); not documented in any record.
founder_or_family: Not documented. Residents name the zamindar as Binoy Kumar Majumdar (Somoy BD, 2022); English Wikipedia names the brothers Minay Kumar and Vinay Kumar as the zamindars who lived there.
architectural_style: Not described beyond a colonial-era residence; sources mention original furniture, a granary (gola ghar), a well and a water-lifting motor.
preservation_status: Unprotected and deteriorating from neglect. Two brothers, Habil and Kabil, live in the house although parts are unsafe (Somoy BD 2022; Wikipedia). Listed as a tourist spot by the Chuadanga district portal.

coordinates_note: Pin found in Google Maps on 14 Oct 2026, from the place's own pin. Matched place 'Chanchra Shiva Temple' (Hindu temple, plus code 46V3+QMC). The palace itself is not on Google Maps; 'Chanchra Rajbari Jame Masjid' (23.1462183, 89.2040193) and 'Chanchra Rajbari Dalmil Jame Mosque' on Raja Bardakanta Road, about 200 m north, carry the Rajbari name and are the best proxy for the palace site. short_description: Seat of the Chanchra rajas, among the most important zamindar families of old Jessore, whose palace stood beside the Shiva temple on the Jashore-Benapole road about 4 km south of Jashore town. The palace has vanished; what visitors see is the 1696 at-chala Shiva temple built by Raja Manohar Ray and its lotus pond, a protected monument still used for worship at Shivaratri and Dol. Historian Satish Chandra Mitra described it in his 1914 history of Jessore and Khulna. This record covers the estate; the temple's 1696 date is not the estate's founding date.
established_era: The district portal says Mahtab Ray established the Chanchra rajas' rule in 1610 (estate); the surviving Shiva temple is dated 1696 by its inscription. The master list's 'late 16th century, Raja Manohar Ray' is not supported.
founder_or_family: Mahtab Ray (founder, d. 1619), then his son Kandarpa Ray (r. 1619-1658), per the Jashore district portal; Raja Manohar Ray built the Shiva temple in 1696 (inscription). Manohar Ray's reign is given as 1658-1705 (Prothom Alo, per the audit) or 1689-1705 (Showcase).
architectural_style: Shiva temple in the Bengal at-chala (eight-roofed) style: a truncated char-chala roof topped by a miniature char-chala, three arched doorways, brick and lime mortar, terracotta facade (Prothom Alo English, Showcase). The palace's style is not recorded.
preservation_status: The palace is gone: Showcase (2020) says no trace of it has been found, and Khoborsangjog (2025) calls the temple the only surviving part of the rajbari. The Shiva temple stands, restored in 2008 to UNESCO guidelines; Showcase notes the terracotta panels were put on in that restoration.

short_description: Birthplace and family home of Michael Madhusudan Dutt, built by his father Rajnarayan Dutta, zamindar of Sagardari, on the bank of the Kapotaksha. The two-storey house is now a Department of Archaeology museum of family belongings (his bed, letters, a first-edition book and Madras-period items) with a library, the poet's statue (1984), a kitchen, guesthouse and pond. Madhumela is held here in the last week of January on his birth anniversary. The audit lists 'M.M. Dutta Bari Museum, Keshabpur' as an omission from the project's research list.
established_era: Early 19th century; built by Rajnarayan Dutta, the poet's father (Keshabpur Upazila portal). No construction year found.
founder_or_family: Rajnarayan Dutta, made zamindar of Sagardari, built the house (Keshabpur Upazila portal). The family came from Gopalpur, Tala (Satkhira), where great-grandfather Ramkishore Dutta lived.
architectural_style: Two-storey main house with tiled roof, red brick walls and wooden doors and windows, plus single-storey outbuildings (Daily Star Bangla, upazila portal).
preservation_status: Preserved as a museum and library. Declared an archaeological site on 26 Oct 1965; renovated by the Department of Archaeology in 1968 with a boundary wall, gate and reception building.

Taxes were collected here and defaulters punished, per local accounts. It is a fort-like residence of a Mughal official, not a zamindar house, and is recorded here because the audit lists it as an omission and it pairs with Sagardari.
established_era: 1649, by the plaque (Daily Star 2009, Keshabpur Upazila portal). Banglapedia says 17th century.
founder_or_family: Safsi (Shafsi) Khan, Mughal commander or governor at Jessore under Subahdar Shah Shuja (upazila portal, Daily Star). Banglapedia calls it the 'palace of Nawab Mir Jumla'.
architectural_style: Mughal bathhouse: rectangular, four rooms and four domes, 4.6 ft walls about 20 ft high, cisterns on the east side, a well and an underground store room (Daily Star 2009, Khoborsangjog 2025).
preservation_status: The hammam stands inside a walled enclosure; the rest of the Nawab Bari is gone. Protected archaeological site since 1996. Cracked and overgrown in 2009 (Daily Star).

preservation_status: Largely lost. The house has been sold and few remains are visible; two fragile temples, two large ponds and a paved ghat survive, and bricks are stolen at night (Amar Barta, 2022).

short_description: A riverside mansion on the north bank of the Nabaganga, 3 km from Jhenaidah town, built in 1822-29 by Salimullah Chowdhury, son of a Naldanga raj dewan who earned the Chowdhury title in its service. A verse inscription on the gate records the start (1229 BS), the finish (1236 BS), the cost of Tk 75,000 and a Calcutta builder. Locals tell of a tunnel under the river and of a many-headed date palm. It was sold around Partition, so some call it Selim Chowdhury's house.
established_era: Begun 1229 BS and finished 1236 BS (about 1822-1829 CE), per the gate inscription (Prothom Alo 2020, Vromon Guide). Banglapedia: 'house of Salim Chowdhury (1822)'.
founder_or_family: Zamindar Salimullah Chowdhury, called 'Miya Saheb', whose father Badhui Biswas was a dewan of the Naldanga raj; the inscription names his wife Bibi Ashrafunnesa. Bought around 1947 by Selim Chowdhury (Prothom Alo).
architectural_style: Two-storey brick and lime-surki house, about 82 x 66 ft, 16 rooms, 25-inch walls, with a marble-lined rooftop prayer room (chilekotha) (Prothom Alo).
preservation_status: Standing but deteriorating for lack of conservation (Prothom Alo 2020); listed among Jhenaidah's 21 gazetted heritage sites and described as neglected (Financial Express, 2026). Private property.

short_description: Seat of the Naldanga rajas of Mahmudshahi pargana, one of old Jessore's great estates, on the Begbati river about 18 km from Jhenaidah town. The palace has almost vanished, but its temple group on some 20 acres survives and is busy with worship: the Siddheshwari temple (first built 1656) and temples to Kali, Lakshmi, Ganesh, Durga, Tara, Vishnu and Rajeshwari. The estate passed to the government in 1955 after the family left for India. A 2026 study argues Naldanga was an intermediate regional authority, more than a zamindari but not a sovereign state. A modern 'Naldanga Rajbari Resort' nearby is a private amusement park, not the historic site.
established_era: Title of Raja given to Chandicharan Deb Roy in 1656 (English Wikipedia); the Siddheshwari temple was first built in 1656 (Daily Star). The family traced itself much further back. The master list's 'Raja Srimanta Dev Ray, 16th century' was not found in any source.
founder_or_family: Deb Roy family of Naldanga, descended per family history from Haladhar Bhattacharji; Chandicharan Deb Roy received the Raja title in 1656. Last raja: Pramatha Bhusan Deb Roy (1858-c. 1941), Raja Bahadur from 1913 (Wikipedia, Daily Star).
architectural_style: Group of tall brick temples, 35-40 ft, with 3.5-4 ft walls; the Vishnu (Pancha Debota) temple is two-storey and about 60 ft (Daily Star 2009). Palace style not recorded.
preservation_status: Palace largely gone; crops grow on its site and its furniture was auctioned (Daily Star 2009). Seven of eight temples stand; six were being restored by the Naldanga Mandir Committee in 2020, while the Rajeshwari and Vishnu temples were in poor condition. Listed among Jhenaidah's 21 gazetted heritage sites (Financial Express, 2026).

short_description: The house of the Shikdar zamindars at Abaipur, on the Magura (Sreepur) border of Shailkupa, built by Ramsundar Shikdar on some 400 bigha. A later family member, Ramchandra, added a sub-registry office, a large bazar and a theatre hall, and the area became known as Shikdar Street. Descendants keep family objects: a gramophone, a stone or wooden hookah, a sword, an old Srimad Bhagavatam, an esraj, two sal-wood shrines and pieces of a zari Benarasi sari. Abaipur Ramsundar Secondary School (1889) is named after him.
established_era: Early 19th century, about 200 years old (Doinik Voreralo, 2022).
founder_or_family: Zamindar Ramsundar Shikdar, a jute merchant and founder of 'Shikdar & Company'; his grandfather Kartik received the Shikdar title from the Nawab of Murshidabad (the family's earlier title was Tilikundu). Later descendant: Rajkumar Shikdar (Doinik Voreralo).
architectural_style: Two-storey house ranged around courtyards, said to have had about 350 rooms, within a brick and surki wall (Vromon Guide, Doinik Voreralo).
preservation_status: Standing. Part houses the union land office and part is used by descendants (Vromon Guide); Doinik Voreralo says it is privately owned and no descendants now live there.

name_en: Acharya Prafulla Chandra Ray's House, Raruli
alternate_names: Sir PC Roy House; P. C. Ray's ancestral house; রাড়ুলী জমিদার বাড়ি; Raruli Zamindar Bari; স্যার পিসি রায়ের বাড়ি
coordinates_note: Pin found in Google Maps on 15 Oct 2026, from the place's own pin. Matched place 'Sir PC Roy House' (history museum) at Raruli.
short_description: Birthplace and family house of the chemist Acharya Sir Prafulla Chandra Ray (1861-1944) at Raruli on the Kapotaksha, next to Katipara in Paikgachha. His father Harish Chandra Raychowdhury was a zamindar (English Wikipedia) who founded a girls' school named after his mother in 1850. The Department of Archaeology protects the main house, the natmandir and the kachari building; land around them was encroached after 1971 and part is under litigation. Locals are asking for a science heritage centre and museum.
established_era: 19th century; not dated. Prafulla Chandra Ray was born here on 2 August 1861; his father founded Bhuvanmohini Balika Bidyalaya in 1850 (Daily Star Bangla 2026).
founder_or_family: The Raychowdhury family; Harish Chandra Raychowdhury (d. 1893), described by English Wikipedia as a Kayastha zamindar, father of the chemist Acharya Prafulla Chandra Ray.
architectural_style: Old brick complex with a sadar mahal (main house), natmandir, kachari bari and a two-storey northern building (Daily Star Bangla 2026). Not otherwise described.
preservation_status: Protected by the Department of Archaeology since 7 November 1996 (sadar mahal, natmandir and kachari bari). Parts are collapsing; repairs in 2012-13 and 2014-15 and a Tk 39 lakh renovation from December 2025. 1.43 of 3.42 acres are under the Department; the rest is in a court case (Daily Star Bangla, Aug 2026). No museum yet.

alternate_names: Rabindra Smriti Bhavan, Dakshindihi; Dakshindihi Rabindra Memorial Museum; দক্ষিণডিহি রবীন্দ্র স্মৃতি জাদুঘর; Dakkhindihi Rabindra Complex; Beni Madhab Roy Chowdhury's house
coordinates_note: Pin found in Google Maps on 15 Oct 2026, from the place's own pin. Matched place 'Dakkhindihi Rabindra Complex' (history museum).
short_description: The two-storey house of Beni Madhab Roy Chowdhury at Dakshindihi, about 19-20 km from Khulna city and about 3 km north-west of Phultala upazila centre. His daughter Bhabatarini, renamed Mrinalini Devi, married Rabindranath Tagore in 1883; Tagore's mother Sarada Devi and his aunt Tripura Sundari Devi also came from the village. The family moved to Kolkata in 1940 and exchanged the property; it was later occupied, recovered by the district administration on 7 September 1995 and handed to the Department of Archaeology in 2000. Busts of Tagore and Mrinalini Devi and the 'Mrinalini Mancha' stage stand in front; inside are photographs, a small library and displays. A Tagore festival is held on 25-27 Baishakh. This is a literary-memorial house, not a zamindar palace.
established_era: 19th century; not precisely dated. The house belonged to Beni Madhab Roy Chowdhury, whose daughter Mrinalini Devi married Rabindranath Tagore on 9 December 1883 (English Wikipedia).
founder_or_family: Beni Madhab Roy Chowdhury, Tagore's father-in-law, described as a Jessore landlord (English Wikipedia); later his son Nagendranath (Daily Star Bangla) or Narendranath 'Felu Babu' (English Wikipedia) Roy Chowdhury.
architectural_style: Two-storey brick house: ground floor two rooms and eight windows under a 13 ft ceiling; first floor four rooms, 21 windows, seven doors and wall almirahs (English Wikipedia).
preservation_status: Protected by the Department of Archaeology and run as a museum since 2016 (opened for ticketed visits in April 2016, declared a museum on 10 May 2016). Renovated in 2011-12; the larger Rabindra Complex plan (research centre, auditorium, rest house) is still unfinished (Daily Star Bangla, 2023; Bangla Tribune).

alternate_names: Barobari; বড়বাড়ি; Bedkashi Garh; Pratapaditya's fort, Koyra
coordinates_note: From Bangladesh's 2023 UNESCO Tentative List submission, site AGD.21 (22°18'34.15"N 89°18'25.01"E). Not found in Google Maps on 15 Oct 2026 (English and Bangla names); the nearest named place is 'খালাস খাঁর দিঘি' (Khalas Khan Dighi, 22.30380, 89.29914), about 1 km west-south-west, and the Uttar Bedkashi village pin is at 22.30247, 89.29897.
short_description: A walled earthwork-and-brick enclosure at Barobari in Uttar Bedkashi union, on the edge of the Sundarbans, known locally as Pratapaditya's fort. Surviving wall sections enclose about 335 m by 275 m; carved stones weighing 50-100 kg with deities, plants and animals, a stone bearing two possibly Brahmi letters, buried foundations 10-15 ft deep and three old ponds (Sheel, Padma and Dui Sotiner Pukur) have been reported. The nearby Khalas Khan Dighi (about 1,050 x 600 ft) is dated by the Prothom Alo writers to about 1445-50. Bangladesh included the site in its 2023 UNESCO Tentative List submission as AGD.21. It is a fortified site, not a zamindar house.
established_era: Disputed. Prothom Alo (2022) dates the fort to about 1587-95 CE in the Pratapaditya tradition but argues the ruins are older; the UNESCO Tentative List submission gives c. 9th-18th century and says archaeological evidence points to pre-13th-century occupation, with the brick walls probably later.
founder_or_family: Popularly attributed to Raja Pratapaditya of Jashore (with his uncle Basanta Roy); several archaeologists reject the attribution (Prothom Alo). UNESCO's text presents it as popular tradition only.
architectural_style: Rectangular brick enclosure, overlain by mud, about 335 m x 275 m (UNESCO), with buried brick structures and carved stone blocks inside and outside.
preservation_status: Ruined, privately owned land (UNESCO). Residents dig out old bricks for building (Prothom Alo).
