coordinates_note: Pin found in Google Maps on 15 Oct 2026, from the place's own pin. Matched place 'Shilaidaha Rabindra Kuthibari' (historical place museum). English Wikipedia's infobox (23.919641, 89.219961) is about 35 m away.
short_description: The Tagore family's estate house on the south bank of the Padma at Shilaidaha. Rabindranath Tagore first came here in November 1889 to take charge of the family zamindari and lived here at intervals until 1901 (Banglapedia; the audit reports the Department of Archaeology gives 1889-1901). He wrote Sonar Tari, Chitra, Chaitali, Katha O Kahini, Kshanika and most of Naibedya and Kheya here, and began translating Gitanjali into English here in 1912 (Banglapedia). The house stands in about 11 acres of orchards with two ponds, a flower garden and a boundary wall with a south gate. It was acquired by the government under the 1950 State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and is now a museum of Tagore's photographs, furniture, boats and personal items.
established_era: The Tagore family's estate seat from the 19th century. Dwarkanath Tagore became owner of the zamindari in 1807 through Ramlochan Tagore's will; an indigo kuthi built by a planter named Shelly stood in the village before the Tagores acquired it in the mid-19th century (Banglapedia). Banglapedia's Kumarkhali page dates the Kuthibari to 1862. The present building was rebuilt after the original was lost to river erosion, reusing its materials (Banglapedia); the rebuild date is not given.
founder_or_family: Tagore family of Jorasanko (Dwarkanath Tagore as owner from 1807; Rabindranath Tagore managed the estate from 1889). Wikipedia names Ramlochan Tagore as founder.
architectural_style: Colonial terraced bungalow of brick, timber, corrugated tin and Raniganj tiles, with a pitched gabled roof over the centre and a short pyramidal crest (Banglapedia). Wikipedia calls it Indo-Saracenic.
preservation_status: Preserved. Protected national monument run as a museum by the Department of Archaeology (museum since 1986 per Wikipedia). Parts of a protective embankment collapsed in 2018 and 2022 (Wikipedia).

The family's Radhakanta Lakshmi Narayan Jiu temple, endowed with 10 acres, is about 100 yards from the house, and they also founded the Siddheswari Kali temple at Dariapur. Only part of the L-shaped two-storey house stands, including a small under-stair room locals call 'Aadhar Kutha', where rebels were said to be held (oral claim). preservation_status: Mostly destroyed and overgrown; the site is a raised mound. Locals clean it each year for the family deity's festival. Unprotected. The family temples were vandalised in 2017 and the Dariapur Kali temple robbed in 2022.

short_description: Capital of Raja Sitaram Ray, who took Naldi, Satair and Bhati in 1688 and built a moated brick fort at Mohammadpur, about 500 m from the upazila office, with the Madhumati about 1 km east. Mohammadpur fell to the Mughals and Sitaram died in Murshidabad in October 1714. Surviving pieces include the Kachharibari, the Dol Mancha, the Toshakhana and palace remains, a rebuilt Dashabhuja temple, the Padmapukur pond and the huge Ram Sagar tank (2,400 by 900 ft); a pancharatna Krishna temple stands at Kanainagar to the west. The audit's advice is followed here: it is a palace-fort and archaeological site, not a zamindar house in the usual sense.
established_era: Late 17th century: Sitaram became ruler of Naldi, Satair and Bhati in 1688 and then built a fortified capital at Mohammadpur (Wikipedia).
founder_or_family: Raja Sitaram Ray (died 1714), a zamindar who rebelled against Mughal authority.
architectural_style: Mughal-era brick buildings with terracotta plaques (Daily Star, 2011); square fort of at least 1,300 ft a side, built of earthen brick, with a moat (Wikipedia).
preservation_status: Ruins. The Department of Archaeology gazetted the site as a protected antiquity on 15 Apr 2010 and has repaired the Kachharibari and Dol Mancha (Sthapattya O Nirman, 2023). Encroached: of 163 decimals on record only 35 hold structures; 74 are occupied by locals and 18 families live on 54 (Daily Star 2011; Sthapattya 2023). In Aug 2026 the department proposed protection for the Toshakhana (BSS).

short_description: Remains of the Pal Chowdhury zamindars' house about 1 km north of Sreepur upazila town, on the left of the Sreepur-Sachilapur road beside Sreepur Mohila College. Tradition says Sarada Ranjan Pal Chowdhury bought the estate from Nawab Alivardi Khan and that his daughter Bibha married Udayaditya, son of Pratapaditya of Jessore, whose help built the house; Tagore's novel 'Bou Thakuranir Haat' is locally said to draw on her. The dates do not fit: Pratapaditya died about 1611 and Alivardi ruled 1740-56. A 2026 archaeological survey recorded the surviving gate in detail and called the site critically endangered.
established_era: Surviving gate dated to the 19th century on architectural grounds, about 225 years old (Khatun and Islam, 2026). Local claims of 300-400 years and the '15th century' dates in travel pieces are unsupported.
founder_or_family: Sarada Ranjan (Sardaranjan) Pal Chowdhury, who by local tradition bought the zamindari from Nawab Alivardi Khan.
architectural_style: Colonial-era; the surviving two-storey south-facing gate has octagonal bamboo-knot pillars, a pointed arch, two small domes over the passage, four guard rooms and dentil cornice decoration (Khatun and Islam, 2026). The main house is gone.
preservation_status: Ruined and unprotected. Only the gate (upper floor destroyed) and part of the west boundary wall survive; a brick and a tin-roofed building stand where the house was. The owners live in Dhaka; a plate on the gate gives their phone number and entry needs their permission (Khatun and Islam, 2026). No Department of Archaeology work (The NRD, 2026).

short_description: One of the best-known indigo factories in Bangladesh, on the bank of the Kajla river in Amjhupi, Meherpur Sadar. It was built for processing indigo for export and was later used as a court office of the East India Company (Financial Express). After zamindari abolition the Midnapore Company's holding passed to the district administration, then the district council and the upazila administration; it was declared a tourist site on 13 May 1978 and the Tourism Ministry took responsibility in 2015 (BSS, 2025). Locals say the conspirators against Nawab Siraj ud-Daulah held their last meeting here before Plassey, but the kuthi did not exist in 1757 and historian Aminul Islam rejects the story (Financial Express). The main building has 15 rooms, a hall, a dance room and a dining room, set in a large mango orchard with a bathing ghat on the Kajla (Daily Star Bangla, 2025).
established_era: Usually dated to around 1815 or later; exact date uncertain (Meherpur District portal via the audit). BSS (2025) estimates 1800-1815.
founder_or_family: Indigo planters of the East India Company era. The French colonist Louis Bonnaud is credited with first bringing indigo cultivation to the area (Financial Express). British officials Simpson and Ferguson lived here (BSS, 2025); records name planters Kenny, Simpson, James Heel, Fergun Crawford, Warts and Hamilton (Financial Express). Later held by the Midnapore Company until zamindari abolition (BSS, 2025).
architectural_style: Colonial planter's house (not described in detail by any source found)
preservation_status: Preserved. The main building was remodelled and is supervised by the Department of Archaeology with Ansar guards and caretakers; the nayeb's house is largely destroyed and the grounds lack a boundary wall (BSS, Oct 2025).

A mango garden adjoins it and a ruined church stands to the north-west (English Wikipedia). The district administration took back the land and developed the DC Eco Park around the ruins, with an artificial lake, a waterfall, sculptures and flower gardens (Daily Star Bangla, 2023).

short_description: The Narail Roys were the dominant zamindars of the Narail area from 1791. After the 1793 Permanent Settlement Kali Shankar Ray bought up lands auctioned from Rani Bhabani's Natore estate and governed them from Narail. The family funded early schools in the town, including what became Narail Government Victoria College and its collegiate school, and gave the town its Kuriddobe playing field. The family left for Kolkata after Partition (1947), returned briefly around 1950-52, and left again when zamindari was abolished. Most of the palace complex has since gone; what visitors see today are scattered remains, chiefly the Badhaghat on the Chitra, which the district administration has tiled and fenced, and the old stone temple.
established_era: Late 18th century (lineage from 1791)
founder_or_family: Rupram (Ruparam) Ray began the lineage in 1791 as a taluqdar under Rani Bhabani of Natore; his son Kali Shankar Ray bought auctioned Natore lands after the 1793 Permanent Settlement and made Narail his headquarters. short_description: A Mughal-type bathhouse at Bangshipur, Ishwaripur, part of the Bonghipur-Ishwaripur-Dhumghat archaeological cluster in Bangladesh's 2023 UNESCO Tentative List submission. Banglapedia describes three chambers (pre-bath, bath, and a reservoir that doubled as a water heater) and dates it to the early 17th century; local tradition links it to Pratapaditya's palace. Banglapedia's Shyamnagar page calls it 'six domed'. Recorded separately from the palace, as the audit asks.
established_era: Undated. Banglapedia assumes the Mughal period, early 17th century; English Wikipedia and a bangladesh.com blog say late 16th century, by Pratapaditya.
founder_or_family: Attributed to Pratapaditya (English Wikipedia); Banglapedia names no builder.
architectural_style: Rectangular bathhouse with three chambers (pre-bath, bath, and water reservoir-cum-heater) under a dome (Banglapedia 'Hammam').
preservation_status: Ruined monument; listed as AGD.27 in Bangladesh's 2023 UNESCO Tentative List submission. Department of Archaeology protection not confirmed here.

alternate_names: Dhumghat Rajbari; ধুমঘাট রাজবাড়ি; Maharaja Pratapaditya's capital

short_description: The ruins at Ishwaripur, near the Jessoreshwari temple, that local tradition calls Maharaja Pratapaditya's palace. The Daily Star's 'Pratapaditya Trail' (2019) describes a two-storey front block and a three-storey rear block in ruins, a pond linked to the story of Pratapaditya's death, and a brick 'hawa khana' beside it. Ishwaripur village, 64 km south of Satkhira town on the old Ichamati (now Kadamtali canal), also has the Hammamkhana, Jessoreshwari temple, the five-domed Tenga mosque, the Chanda Bhairab temple and the site of a church the Portuguese built in 1599. The master list's 'Dhumghat Rajbari' and 'Ishwaripur Zamindar Bari' both point here; Dhumghat's own site was not located in any source checked.
established_era: Late 16th century by tradition. English Wikipedia says Pratapaditya's capital was first at Dhumghat and then at Ishwaripur, 1590-1610; the Daily Star (2019) says historical accounts of the palace are vague.
founder_or_family: Raja Pratapaditya of Jashore, one of the Baro Bhuiyan, by tradition (Daily Star 2019). The UNESCO submission notes there is no empirical evidence for several Pratapaditya attributions in the cluster.
architectural_style: Two sections survive: a two-storey front building and a three-storey back building (Daily Star 2019). Not otherwise described.
preservation_status: Ruins (Daily Star 2019). Protection status not found.

alternate_names: Jeshoreshwari Kali Temple; Joseshwari Mandir; যশোরেশ্বরী মন্দির; Jessoreshwari Shakti Peeth
coordinates_note: Google Maps place 'Jessoreshwari Mandir Complex' (historical place, plus code 8447+F42, 52 reviews), read on 15 Oct 2026, agrees to within about 10 m with the English Wikipedia infobox (22°18′22″N 89°06′46″E). A second Google place, 'Shree Jeshoreswari Maa Shaktipith Temple' (22.29980, 89.11564), is about 730 m south-east and was not used.
short_description: One of the 51 Shakti Peeths of Hindu tradition (one of six in Bangladesh), where Sati's palm is said to have fallen. Pratapaditya is said to have begun Kali worship here after his general found a palm-shaped stone, and the temple is the best-known part of the Ishwaripur group linked to him. It was partly destroyed in 1971 and renovated in 2021; Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi worshipped here on 27 March 2021, and the crown he gave was stolen in October 2024. Worship is held on Tuesdays and Saturdays at noon, with Kali Puja and a fair in autumn. A temple, not a palace; recorded because the audit asks to split it from the Dhumghat entry.
established_era: Traditionally late 12th century (built by a brahmin, Anari), renovated by Lakshman Sen in the 13th century and rebuilt by Pratapaditya in the 16th century (Daily Star Bangla 2021). English Wikipedia says the original date is unknown.
founder_or_family: Tradition names Anari, a brahmin; Lakshman Sen and Pratapaditya renovated it.
architectural_style: Ratna-style temple (English Wikipedia infobox), with the pillars of a ruined natmandir beside it; traditionally a '100-door' temple.
preservation_status: Active temple; partly demolished in 1971, renovated in 2021. Only the pillars of the natmandir remain (English Wikipedia).

name_en: Nakipur Zamindar Bari (Haricharan Roy Chowdhury's House)
alternate_names: Nakipur Jamidar Bari; Haricharan Ray Chowdhury's house; হরিচরণ রায় চৌধুরীর বাড়ি; Shyamnagar Zamindar Bari
coordinates_note: Pin found in Google Maps on 15 Oct 2026, from the place's own pin. Matched place 'Hari Charan Zamindar Bari' (historical landmark, plus code 84P9+P32, 304 reviews). A second Google place for the same site, 'Shyamnagar Jamindar Bari' (84P9+M25), is about 12 m away. A third pin, 'নকিপুর জমিদার বাড়ী' (22.34343, 89.10641, 2 reviews), is about 1.4 km north-west and probably misplaced.
short_description: The house of zamindar Haricharan Roy Chowdhury at Nakipur, about 2 km east of Shyamnagar upazila headquarters and about 72 km from Satkhira town. Built in 1888 on about 12 bigha with gardens, it had a Gopal Dev temple on the middle floor, a Durga mandap, twin Shiva temples, a two-storey eight-pillared nahabat khana (still nearly intact), a clinic, guest and office rooms and a large pond with a stone-paved ghat. The family founded Nakipur Minor School in 1899, now Nakipur Government Haricharan Pilot Model Secondary School, and left for India in 1954.
established_era: 1888 (bdnews24 2021; Dainik Dristipat 2023).
founder_or_family: Zamindar Haricharan Roy Chowdhury, also styled Hari Charan Roy Bahadur (Dainik Dristipat). The family left for India in 1954.
architectural_style: Three-storey L-shaped brick, lime and surki mansion, about 210 ft long, 37 ft wide and 64 ft high, with carved doors and windows, a lion gate and 8 ft verandas (Dainik Dristipat). bdnews24 counts 41 rooms; Dainik Dristipat gives 17 on the ground floor and 5 above, plus an underground part.
preservation_status: Ruined and unprotected. About half the main building has collapsed, doors and windows are gone, trees grow on the walls and salt damage loosens the bricks (Dainik Dristipat, Nov 2023). No Department of Archaeology action reported.

English Wikipedia, drawing on Badru Mohammad Khalequzzaman's history of Tala (2006), describes a long twin-pillared verandah, offices and rooms for palanquins, one of which needed twelve bearers, and notes that the gateway's wall seemed to carry inscriptions or patterns in 1982. founder_or_family: Khan Bahadur Maulvi Qazi Salamatullah Khan of the Qazi zamindars of Tetulia (English Wikipedia).
architectural_style: A long verandah on twin pillars under a crumbling roof at least 3.2 m high, with offices and palanquin rooms; the gateway ('Shingho Doroja') was later renovated in a different style (English Wikipedia).
preservation_status: Ruined: only the main gate and part of one wall survive (the book, 2024, with a photograph of the gateway)

alternate_names: Tetulia Shahi Mosque; তেঁতুলিয়া শাহী মসজিদ; Khan Bahadur Salamatullah Mosque; Tentulia Jami Mosque
coordinates_note: Google Maps place 'Tetulia Shahi Jame Masjid' (mosque, Tentulia Bazar, Paikgacha Rd, 207 reviews), read on 15 Oct 2026, agrees to within about 10 m with the English Wikipedia infobox (22°46′54″N 89°15′05″E). Beware a different 'তেতুলিয়া জামে মসজিদ' far outside Satkhira (24.226, 89.951).
short_description: The zamindar mosque of Tetulia, about 3 km north of Tala upazila sadar beside the Khulna-Paikgachha road. Built in 1858-59 by Qazi Salamatullah Khan, it has a roofed prayer hall of 47 x 30 ft and an open eastern courtyard of 37 x 30 ft (now under a tin roof), holding about 350 worshippers. Family graves, including those of Qazi Mohammad Shafiullah Khan and Khan Sahib Qazi Rizwanullah Khan, are in the mosque cemetery. The ruined family mansion, Salam Manzil, stands nearby and has its own record. Banglapedia lists the mosque as Tala's archaeological heritage.
established_era: 1858-59, from the inscription on the premises (Prothom Alo 2026; English Wikipedia).
founder_or_family: Khan Bahadur Maulvi Qazi Salamatullah Khan, zamindar of Tetulia pargana (Prothom Alo; English Wikipedia).
architectural_style: Mughal revival: six large domes in two rows with smaller domes around them, 20 minarets including four tall corner ones, seven arched doorways and two large round pillars; terracotta leaf, moon and star motifs. Inspired by the Patti mosque in Kolkata; the builder was brought from Delhi (Prothom Alo).
preservation_status: Active congregational mosque. Floors renovated in 1987 with Department of Archaeology funding; much of the terracotta is now painted over and the committee has asked for government help (Prothom Alo, Mar 2026).

Whether this is their seat is inferred from the name only. The family's town house in Mymensingh is a separate record (gouripur-lodge).

That building later housed Atharabari Degree College, which moved out about five years ago. The palace compound also has a puja mandap.

short_description: Seat of the Acharya Chowdhury zamindars, the most powerful family of old Mymensingh, whose estate was split among 16 shareholders. short_description: The Bogura Nawab family's palace stands near Satmatha on the Karatoya. Nawab Abdus Sobhan Chowdhury acquired the land; the estate passed to his daughter Altafunnesa, her son Syed Altaf Ali Chowdhury and his son Mohammed Ali Bogra. From 1998 part of the grounds ran as the Mohammed Ali Palace Museum and an amusement park, with sculpted scenes of the old household by Aminul Karim Dulal. In April 2016 the property was sold to local businessmen; after protests the Department of Archaeology gazetted it as a protected antiquity in May 2016. The project's master list cites a later Prothom Alo report headed 'শেষ পর্যন্ত ভাঙা পড়ছে বগুড়ার ঐতিহ্যবাহী নওয়াব প্যালেস' (finally being demolished) and advises against calling it an open museum; the project could not open that report.

founder_or_family: Nawab Abdus Sobhan Chowdhury, who became zamindar of Bogura by marriage and bought the 3.75-acre Karatoya-bank property from an indigo planter named Abot; title of Nawab granted 20 March 1894. founder_or_family: Majumdar family (Barendra Kayastha), descended from Lohuram Achar; zamindar Kamodoranjan Majumdar, whose sons were Haripada Majumdar (moved to India) and Kalipada Majumdar.
architectural_style: Not documented; the complex had two two-storey buildings and several temples.
preservation_status: Mostly lost: only the dependents' brick house and traces of the Govinda temple remain (Pundrokotha, 2022).

alternate_names: Madla Jamidar Bari; Sarkar family zamindar bari, Madla
coordinates_note: Pin found in Google Maps on 15 Oct 2026. Matched place 'Madla Jamidar Bari' (historical landmark, 4.1 stars, 30 reviews, plus code RC45+QVH). A 'Jamidar Bari Playground' is about 120 m south (24.8058316, 89.4097467).
short_description: The Sarkar family's house stands on about 33 bighas in the Madla Bandar area of Shajahanpur, near Madla hat, the union health centre and post office. Until 1971 it was enclosed by a high wall with seven main gates guarded by paiks, with a ghat-lined pond in front, a tree-lined approach, a jalsa ghar and a fort-like block on the west. The house was looted during the 1971 war; gold, furniture, doors and windows were taken. A month-long Rath festival was held in zamindari days and the family still holds an annual puja. The Department of Archaeology's Rajshahi office said in 2021 that it had little information on the site and would inspect it.
established_era: Claimed to be about 400 years old and Mughal-era; no documentary support (see conflicts). Zamindari ended in 1950.
founder_or_family: Zamindar Biswanath Sarkar, said to have received the zamindari from the Nawab of Bogura; succeeded by his sons Surendra Nath and Narendra Nath Sarkar, then Kshitindra Nath and Bimalendu Nath Sarkar.
architectural_style: Walled compound with a lion gate (singhadwar), a jalsa ghar (music and dance hall) and a fort-like structure on the west; style not described.
preservation_status: Ruined; the main gate, parts of the wall and old trees survive and descendants still use the site (Joy Jugantor / Bangladesh Pratidin 2021; Sangbad Bulletin 2025).

short_description: The house of Syed Torab Ali Chowdhury stood on the west bank of a pond west of Murail madrasa. Before he died in 1868 he endowed the estate as a waqf; Syed Abdul Majid was the first mutawalli, with a Kayastha named Raghunath managing while he was a minor, and Hashem Ali Chowdhury is the present mutawalli. Three roofless structures survive among creepers; the kachari is gone. South of the house stood an elephant stable for two elephants, whose leg-chains are kept as mementos. Locals say the elephants were buried beside an old unidentified tree west of the house, the 'Achin Gachh', which is also listed by the upazila as a tourist spot; the burial is local belief, not established.
established_era: 19th century or earlier; Syed Torab Ali Chowdhury died in 1868.
founder_or_family: Syed Torab Ali Chowdhury, zamindar of a Bogura pargana, who made his property a waqf before his death in 1868 (Pundrokotha, citing Bogura records).
architectural_style: Lime-mortar brick buildings; style not described.
preservation_status: In ruins: three partial structures with collapsed roofs, overgrown; the earthen kachari building has gone (Pundrokotha 2022; Dhaka Mail 2023).

short_description: On the Pagla river about 25 km from Chapainawabganj town, beside Kansat, the country's largest mango market. Originally called Surjya Garh, it became a union land office after 1971 and then stood empty. A 1940s clash between the last zamindar and Muslim tenants led by the Chowdhurys of Shyampur is reported one-sidedly in the sources. Two local name stories (a King Kangsa, and cannon shots giving 'kan sat') are folklore.
established_era: Built in 1867 (Daily Star 2017, citing a local historian; RisingBD 2025).
founder_or_family: Surjya Kanta, a zamindar who moved from Muktagachha, Mymensingh; sons Shashi Kanta and Shitangshu Kanta, the last zamindar, who left for Kolkata after 1947 (Daily Star 2017). The family also owned the Kansat 'Rajar Bagan' mango orchard (Prothom Alo 2021).
architectural_style: Two-storey, richly decorated mansion with 16 rooms on 2.24 acres (Daily Star 2017; RisingBD 2025).
preservation_status: Long neglected and damaged; the Department of Archaeology lists it and in 2025 tendered Tk 16.14 lakh of repairs to the boundary wall, building, doors and windows (RisingBD, Jun 2025). Whether the work is finished is not known.

Travel sites describe a two-storey U-shaped main block with about 17 rooms, a smaller eastern block where elephants were kept, horse and elephant stables, staff quarters, a graveyard, a Kali temple and a pond in the north-west corner, on about 15 bighas still farmed and gardened by the heirs. Parts of the estate reportedly went to India at Partition. The Dhaka Times (2016) mentions a Tk 5 entry charge collected by a local preservation committee.

architectural_style: Two-storey U-shaped main building (Vromon Guide); style not described.

alternate_names: Balihar Zamindar Bari; বলিহার জমিদার বাড়ি; Bolihar Rajbari
coordinates_note: Pin found in Google Maps on 15 Oct 2026, from the place's own pin. Matched 'Balihar Rajbari' (historical landmark, 384 reviews). 'Bolihar Jomidar Bari Gate House' (90 reviews) is in the same compound at 24.8472696, 88.8079954. A second 'Balihar Rajbari' listing with no category or reviews about 350 m SW (24.844585, 88.8058876) opens first on a plain search; do not use it.
short_description: About 18 km west of Naogaon town, the Balihar estate covered 3.5 acres with three buildings and two temples; one building has collapsed. A double-storey gateway leads to a two-storey palace with a front kachari and a rear andarmahal around an inner courtyard. Rajendra Roy built the Rajeshwari Durga temple (1823), flanked by two Shiva temples with terracotta borders, and the poet-zamindar Krishnendra Roy built the Krishna Kali temple (1889). Looted in 1971, the palace later housed a high school (1979) and a college hostel (1994).
established_era: Family history said to run from the late 15th or late 17th century (TBS gives both); the surviving temples are dated 1823 and 1889. The palace's own building date is not documented.
founder_or_family: Nrisingha Chakraborty, a Brahmin from Bikrampur (Dhaka), who rose under a Khan zamindar of Balihar, married his patron's daughter and received a taluk as dowry (TBS 2022). The last zamindar, Kumar Bimalendu Roy (11th generation), left for India after the 1950 abolition. The district portal says the family's jagir came by a sanad of Emperor Aurangzeb (reported by an AI-generated audit; the sanad itself has not been seen).
architectural_style: Indo-European: Greco-Roman pediments, French-style coupled columns, Roman, Venetian and Mughal pointed arches, jaali work and double-shuttered wooden frames (TBS 2022).
preservation_status: Abandoned and dilapidated; ceilings and wall layers crumbling, residential part restricted, Rajeshwari temple building inaccessible. In 2022 the deputy commissioner had written to the Department of Archaeology; no restoration was reported (TBS 2022).

short_description: Near Bhabanipur Bazar on the Chhoto Jamuna in Shahagola union, about 24 km south of Naogaon town. The palace had five courtyards and 45 rooms, three family temples (Durga, Gopinath, Basanti), a paved pond, a music house (Gaan Bari) and a baithakkhana used for arbitration. Priyashankar dug ponds for tenants and built a theatre hall. The family's 1910 school became Bhabanipur G.S. High School.
established_era: Not documented; the family's school dates from 1910.
founder_or_family: Family account: Raghuram Shur -> Kalinath -> Girija Shankar Chowdhury -> Priyashankar Chowdhury, who expanded the estate. Priyashankar moved to Kolkata around 1968; his fourth son Pratapshankar stayed and died in 2005; his son Abhijit Chowdhury lives on site (Jagonews24 2016; Bangladesh Pratidin 2021 via audit).
architectural_style: Described as Roman in style, noted for its pillars; 5 courtyards and 45 rooms (Jagonews24 2016).
preservation_status: Mostly collapsed; doors, windows and sal beams looted after it was listed as enemy property, and bricks removed by locals. Part is still the family's home (Jagonews24 2016; Bangladesh Pratidin, Apr 2021).

alternate_names: Dubalhati Zamindar Bari; দুবলহাটি জমিদার বাড়ি; Dublahati Rajbari
coordinates_note: Pin found in Google Maps on 15 Oct 2026, from the place's own pin. Matched 'Dubolhati Rajbari / দুবলহাটি রাজবাড়ি' (castle/historical landmark, about 644 reviews).
short_description: About 6 km southwest of Naogaon town, the seat of what Banglapedia calls the earliest zamindar family of greater Rajshahi. The palace had four sections (theatre hall, kachari, zenana and kitchen) and about 100 rooms on two floors over 2.45 acres, with a pond on each side. Local tradition says the marshy estate paid its Mughal revenue in koi fish, 22 kahons a year. Haranath Roy Chowdhury founded a free English school here in 1864 and endowed what became Rajshahi College.
established_era: Zamindari founded in the Mughal period by imperial sanad; the present palace probably dates from the end of the 19th century (Banglapedia), rebuilt after the 1897 earthquake (Dhaka Tribune).
founder_or_family: Jagat Ram Roy, a salt (and molasses) dealer from Jajneswarpur, Murshidabad, who settled at Kasba, 3.5 km north of Dubalhati (Banglapedia). Krishnanath Roy held the estate at the 1793 Permanent Settlement; Raja Bahadur Haranath Roy Chowdhury (died 1891) was its most prominent zamindar; Amarendra Nath Roy Chowdhury was the last (Banglapedia).
architectural_style: Colonial or Indo-European north frontage with Corinthian columns, floral pediment and a carved British royal crest; terracotta-decorated arches on the inner veranda (Banglapedia; Dhaka Tribune).
preservation_status: Severely dilapidated: upper floors and the west wing of the Baro Dalan have collapsed and floors are reduced to debris. A Department of Archaeology signboard says it is protected (Dhaka Tribune, 2026). Dubalhati union's portal (updated Jan 2026) calls it on the verge of destruction (via an AI-generated audit).

founder_or_family: Local elders say the family descended from the Natore Raj line; the last raja was Annada Prasanna Lahiri Bahadur, who had four sons and a daughter (Amar Desh 2025). Called the 'Pagla Raja' family because many members were short-tempered.

preservation_status: Almost gone: parts of two temples stand; the last surviving section is a cattle shed, the union land office occupies part of the land, and the rest is encroached and overgrown (Amar Desh, Nov 2025).

Later holders include Shaymanath (died 1878 aged 24), Khitishchandra (Bara taraf) and Rai Bahadur Narayanchandra Raichowdhury (Chhota taraf) (Banglapedia).

preservation_status: Main building preserved as a tourist site with events on Tagore's birth and death anniversaries; adjoining buildings ruined; the Rabindrasarobar pond is silted up (Banglapedia).

coordinates_note: Pin found in Google Maps on 15 Oct 2026, from the place's own pin. Matched 'Natore Rajbari / নাটোর রাজবাড়ী' (historical landmark, 4,395 reviews, CX9R+XQ, Rajbari Rd). Agrees with the Wikipedia infobox (24.4202, 88.9915) to about 50 m.
short_description: Headquarters of the Natore Raj, once one of the largest zamindaris in Bengal. Ramjiban made Natore his seat in the early 18th century and built most of the complex; after Ramkanta's death in 1748 Rani Bhabani ran the estate and enlarged the palace. The estate split into senior (Boro Torof) and junior (Chhoto Torof) branches after 1797, and the 1897 earthquake destroyed many original buildings. Banglapedia's architectural survey describes a 37.2-acre site ringed by two moats with seven detached palace blocks, temples and tanks. It is now a public park with a Tk 20 ticket, with Shyamsundar and Tarakeshwar temples, the Rani Mahal ruins and the Boro and Chhoto Torof buildings.
established_era: Early 18th century: Raja Ramjiban settled at Natore and built the first palace around 1706-1710 (Wikipedia; Daily Star Bangla, 2026).
founder_or_family: Raja Ramjiban (Ramjivan Moitra), founder of the Natore Raj; enlarged by Rani Bhabani, widow of his adopted son Ramkanta (Banglapedia; Wikipedia).
architectural_style: Neoclassical with Doric, Corinthian and semi-Corinthian columns, triangular pediments, Roman segmental arches and stucco friezes (Banglapedia, Nazimuddin Ahmed).
preservation_status: Mixed. Banglapedia describes seven palace blocks, four in usable condition housing offices and the rest collapsed. Today the grounds are a ticketed park run by the district (Daily Star Bangla, 2026).

short_description: Palace of the Dighapatia Raj, about 3 km north of Natore town. Dayaram Roy, dewan to the Natore Raj, began building here in 1734 on an estate granted for his service; the 1897 earthquake wrecked it and Raja Pramadanath Roy rebuilt it, adding an Italian garden. After Partition it came under government control (1966), served as a governor's residence, and was renamed Uttara Gonobhaban in 1972 as the official northern residence of the head of government. The 41-acre walled and moated compound holds more than 12 buildings, including the main palace, Kumar Palace, kachari, treasury and a clock gate whose clock came from Italy.
established_era: 1734 (construction begun by Dayaram Roy); rebuilt after the 1897 earthquake by Raja Pramadanath Roy (Daily Star Bangla, 2026; Wikipedia).
founder_or_family: Dayaram Roy, dewan of the Natore Raj, who received the estate as a reward (Wikipedia); his descendant Raja Pramadanath Roy rebuilt the palace after 1897.
architectural_style: Indo-Saracenic (Wikipedia); Italian garden with marble statues laid out by Pramadanath Roy.
preservation_status: Well kept. Government northern residence and museum (since 9 March 2018); most of the grounds opened to visitors in 2012 (Daily Star Bangla, 2026).

coordinates_note: Pin found in Google Maps on 15 Oct 2026, from the place's own pin. Matched 'Puthia Rajbari / পুঠিয়া রাজবাড়ী' (historical place, 4,677 reviews, 9R6P+QP, Puthia-Bagha Rd). Separate pins: Pancharatna Govinda temple 24.3616023, 88.837088; Bara Shiva temple ('Boro shive Temple') 24.3640787, 88.8370629; Chhoto Govinda temple 24.3623422, 88.8348386.
short_description: The palace of the five-anna (Panchani) branch of the Puthia Raj, one of the oldest and richest zamindari families of Rajshahi. The government brochure says Raja Man Singh granted the Lashkarpur zamindari in 1576 to the ascetic Vatsacharya, who had it registered to his son Pitambar; the estate was split among Anupnarayan's four sons in 1744 into the five-anna and four-anna (Charani) shares. The current two-storey palace was built in 1895 by Maharani Hemanta Kumari Devi; that date belongs to the building, not to the estate. The palace stands in a temple town: the Bara Govinda (Pancharatna) temple, the 1823 Bara Shiva temple, the Dol mandir (1778) and the Jagannath (Rath) temple are nearby, and the brochure counts 14 protected sites.
established_era: Estate: late 16th century (Mughal grant to Vatsacharya's son Pitambar, 1576 per the government brochure). Present palace: 1895.
founder_or_family: Vatsacharya's family (Puthia Raj). The present Panchani palace was built by Maharani Hemanta Kumari Devi in 1895, in memory of her mother-in-law Maharani Sharatsundari Devi (brochure; Wikipedia).
architectural_style: Indo-European (brochure) or Indo-Saracenic Revival (Wikipedia): two-storey rectangular block with Palladian porticos and semi-Corinthian columns, flat roof on iron beams and wooden rafters.
preservation_status: A Department of Archaeology museum (Puthia Rajbari Museum). Wikipedia reports damaged walls, ruined rooms east and south of the Kachari Angan, and stolen terracotta from the nearby temples.

established_era: Estate: 16th century (Raja Kangsa Narayan). Present palace: after 1660, when Lakshminarayan moved the seat to Taherpur (RU conference volume via the audit).
founder_or_family: Raja Kangsa Narayan Roy of Tahirpur. The present palace is attributed to his descendant Lakshminarayan, not to Kangsa Narayan himself (audit, citing the University of Rajshahi conference volume).
architectural_style: Not documented in the sources read.
preservation_status: Used as a college building (TBS; the Daily Star, 2008, where locals say Taherpur College uses the palace). An 18th-century Durga temple beside it is still in worship.

alternate_names: Dinajpur Raj Palace; দিনাজপুর রাজবাটী; Rajbati; Aina Mahal (main block)
coordinates_note: Pin found in Google Maps on 16 Oct 2026, from the place's own pin. Matched 'Dinajpur Rajbari' (historical place, 2,250 reviews, JMW4+9CC, Bottola Mor-Rajbari Road). short_description: The seat of the Dinajpur Raj on the north-eastern edge of Dinajpur town, a walled and moated complex of about 16.41 acres. A tall arched lion-gate faces west; inside are a painted Krishna temple, outhouses, a flat-roofed temple, and the palace proper, divided into Aina Mahal (the east-facing main block with the Durbar hall, Jalsa ghar, Toshakhana and library), Rani Mahal and Thakurbari Mahal. Banglapedia attributes the main mahals and the moats to Prannath and Ramnath in the 18th century; the palace was damaged in the 1897 earthquake and largely rebuilt by Maharaja Girijanath Ray (Daily Star 2003). After the State Acquisition Act the family left and the palace decayed; furniture and fittings were sold or stolen. The complex also includes two large tanks, a defunct zoo, a tennis court, a kachari and the Kumar House. The Kantajew temple, begun by Prannath, is a separate site about 20 km north and is not part of the complex (audit).
established_era: Multi-phase: main mahals and moats probably 18th century (Maharaja Prannath and his adopted son Ramnath, per Banglapedia); heavily rebuilt after the 1897 earthquake by Maharaja Girijanath Ray (Daily Star 2003). Not a single 16th-century build.
founder_or_family: Dinajpur Raj family. Tradition names Raja Dinaraj (or the early 15th-century Raja Ganesh) as founder; recorded history starts with Srimanta Dutta Chaudhury, zamindar at the end of the 17th century, then his sister's son Sukhdev Ghosh, then Prannath Ray and Ramnath (Daily Star 2003; Banglapedia).
architectural_style: Colonial-era palace with classical orders: east-facing main block about 45.7 m wide with paired Ionic columns, spiral staircases and a parapet relief of two elephants holding a crown; Corinthian-order Krishna temple; flat-roofed temple with semi-Corinthian pillars (Banglapedia; Daily Star 2003).
preservation_status: In ruins: abandoned brick buildings in an advanced stage of disintegration (Banglapedia); roofless with exposed girders in 2003 (Daily Star). The district administration began a debris-clearing drive in October 2025 (Desh Rupantor); no formal restoration found.

short_description: The seat of a Muslim zamindar family on the Punarbhaba south of Dinajpur town. Nabir Mohammad came from Jalpaiguri to trade; his son Ful Mohammad bought estates, took the title Chowdhury, renamed Ekbarpur village Ghughudanga and built the house. The estate ran 18 kacharis and 41 tahsil offices across 11 thanas (Teachers' Portal 2020); most of it fell in India after 1947. In 1971 the family sheltered freedom fighters, and Pakistani forces bombed the house in reprisal. A terracotta gate and parts of the buildings remain; the family later settled in the Eidgah area of Dinajpur town.

founder_or_family: Ful Mohammad Chowdhury, only son of Nabir Mohammad, a trader who came from Jalpaiguri (Teachers' Portal 2020; English Wikipedia citing Azharul Azad Jewel's 'Ghughudangar Zamidar', 2007).
architectural_style: Brick and lime-surki; English Wikipedia calls it Indo-Saracenic Revival. A terracotta-decorated entrance gate survives (Teachers' Portal 2020).
preservation_status: Ruined. The main residence was bombed in 1971 after the family sheltered freedom fighters (English Wikipedia; Teachers' Portal). The 2020 account says the gate and some ground- and first-floor buildings still stand, overgrown.

short_description: Bamandanga was one of the larger Rangpur estates. Banglapedia's 'Bamandanga Zamindari' traces it to Rameswar Mustowfi, secretary to the Cooch Behar Maharaja during the Mughal-Cooch Behar campaign, who received half of chakla Fatehpur; it became Bamandanga pargana. Widows ran it for long stretches (Pabitra Devi was the most capable); the court of wards held it in 1779-1807. Kartik Chandra died in 1842, Nabin Chandra recovered the estate in 1856 and took the title Roy Chowdhury in 1880, and dug Bamandanga lake and several Shiva temples. The last zamindars were Manindrachandra (Rangpur Zamindar Association secretary 1945-50) and Jagatchandra Roy Chowdhury. A 2023 visitor describes the compound as having had a residence, guest house, durbar hall, Durga temple, math and cowshed, almost all near destruction with much land occupied. Banglapedia's Sundarganj page lists the house's remnants and a Bamandanga Shiva temple as heritage.

founder_or_family: Rameswar Mustowfi, a Rarhi Brahmin secretary (mustowfi) to the Maharaja of Cooch Behar, who received half of chakla Fatehpur (later Bamandanga pargana) (Banglapedia, Rangpur portal). Later zamindars took the title Roy Chowdhury from 1880. A 2023 Teachers Portal blog instead names Krishnakanta Roy, a Brahmin of Gaur.
architectural_style: Not documented.
preservation_status: Remnants only: the Sarbananda union portal calls it nearly extinct ('বিলুপ্ত প্রায়'); estate land is occupied (2023 blog).

short_description: Bardhankuthi, earlier Bardhankot, was the headquarters of the large Idrakpur pargana, held by a line of Deb rajas under the Mughals and later known as a zamindar house under the British. The Rangpur portal lists the family as the Ghoraghat (Idrakpur) or Bardhankot zamindari, a Mughal jagir from the early 17th century founded by Raja Bhagaban, a Barendra Kayastha. Bangla Wikipedia credits Raja Bhagaban with the Basudeb temple at Rampur in 1601 and names later rajas Manohar, Raghunath, Harinath and Gaurnath (ruling 1781); the last raja, Shailesh Chandra, moved to India at Partition. Gobindaganj College was built on the palace grounds in 1965, and the remains stand among the college buildings and shade trees. The AI-generated guide's claim that Raja Harinath founded it in the 16th century is not supported: the sources put Harinath several generations after Bhagaban, and an AI-generated audit flags it too.
established_era: Seat of the Idrakpur (Ghoraghat) pargana rajas from the Mughal period; the Rangpur portal dates the family's jagir to the start of the 17th century. Surviving buildings are undated.
founder_or_family: Deb-lineage rajas of Idrakpur pargana. The Rangpur portal names Raja Bhagaban as founder of the Bardhankot (Ghoraghat-Idrakpur) jagirdari; Bangla Wikipedia lists Raja Bhagaban, Manohar, Raghunath, Harinath and Gaurnath (1781). The last raja, Shailesh Chandra, left for India at Partition.
architectural_style: Not documented; the district portal mentions a few ornamented old buildings among the ruins.
preservation_status: Ruins inside a college campus: Gobindaganj College was founded on the site in 1965 and campus growth has left the old buildings near total ruin.

coordinates_note: Google Maps place 'নলডাঙ্গা জমিদারবাড়ি' (historical landmark, 42 reviews), found on 16 Oct 2026. It is about 175 m from Offroad Bangladesh's point (25.4832, 89.4718), so two sources agree. Naldanga railway station is at 25.4809, 89.4743.
short_description: The Lahiris of Naldanga were Brahmin zamindars whose seat lay south-east of Rangpur town, in today's Sadullapur upazila of Gaibandha. The Rangpur district portal traces them to Kashinath Lahiri, confidential secretary to the Cooch Behar Maharaja in 1773-1784; local accounts credit the brothers Shibchandra and Shambhuchandra with building the house, which served as a revenue-collection centre. The family is best known for Tulsi Lahiri, playwright, actor, composer and film-maker of the Bengali stage, born here in 1897 (Banglapedia) and died in Calcutta in 1959. Tulsi Lahiri's father Surendranath decorated the house; sculptures on its front wall were later stolen or carried off and only one survives. A temple ruin stands behind the house, and the Gaibandha heritage list (per an AI-generated audit) mentions a Shiva linga and a bull (brisha) shrine. Amader Shomoy (2018) found the house near collapse with Tulsi Lahiri's descendants still living there; a 2023 Somoy TV report headline says visitors are disappointed by its state (article not readable).
established_era: Family settled at Naldanga at the start of the 19th century (Rangpur district portal); building date not documented.
founder_or_family: Lahiri family (Rarhi Brahmin). The Rangpur portal names Kashinath Lahiri, khas-nabis to the Maharaja of Cooch Behar (served 1773-1784), as founder; Offroad Bangladesh says the brothers Shibchandra and Shambhuchandra founded the house. Shibchandra was the grandfather of the playwright and actor Tulsi Lahiri (1897-1959), whose father Surendranath Lahiri decorated the house.
architectural_style: Not documented; Offroad Bangladesh describes a colourful facade once set with sculptures.
preservation_status: Largely ruined: Amader Shomoy (2018) called the house close to disappearing; descendants still lived on the site then.

short_description: The book lists a Baharband zamindar house in Baharband mohalla, Nageshwari. No source found here describes a house at that address. What the Kurigram district portal does document is the old headquarters of Baharband pargana at Dhamshreni, 3 km east of Ulipur, where Rani Satyabati was zamindar: a Chandi temple dated to Aurangzeb's reign, wrecked in the 1897 earthquake and rebuilt, a ruined Dol Mancha in the courtyard of the priest she appointed, and a Siddheshwari Kali temple. The Rangpur district lineage table says the Baharband zamindari was later held by Kantababu of Kasimbazar. This record stands for the pargana seat; it is not evidence that a palace survives, and the book's Nageshwari address is unresolved.

preservation_status: The old Chandi temple was badly damaged in the 1897 earthquake and a new temple was built; the Dol Mancha is ruined.

Women of the family worshipped there until the family left for India before 1971. Locals say a touchstone and other valuables were stolen from it. Banglapedia lists the 'Gharialdanga Zamindar Bari' among Rajarhat's heritage sites. The date and the family's names are unresolved.

short_description: Seat of the Bakshi zamindars of Naodanga pargana in Phulbari, close to the Indian border. Bangla Wikipedia and a 2021 Teachers' Portal post name Pramodaranjan Bakshi, titled 'Bahadur', as the builder; the family also held Bidyabagish, Shimulbari, Taluk Shimulbari and Kabir Mamud, plus a holding at Panga. Accounts say two of the sons bought a house in Cooch Behar after the 1304 BS (1897) earthquake, and the last zamindar, Bishweshwar Prasad Bakshi, left for India after zamindari abolition. Much of the brickwork has since been taken away; the community puja temple and an annual Dol Purnima fair on the field in front remain. The AI-generated guide's 'arches, defensive walls and Shiva temple ruins' are not supported by any source read here.

short_description: Panga was a Koch vassal house: the Rangpur district lineage table says Narasimha, eldest son of Biswa Singha, founder of Cooch Behar, set up the line at Panga. According to the Kurigram district portal, after Rani Lakshmipriya died, her adopted son Debendra Narayan ran the estate under the title 'Kongor' and it declined until it was destroyed. Today only broken brick, a stone-paved pond and an almost intact kachari building remain in Chhinai union, with the Pangeshwari temple nearby. Two Mughal-era cannons from the rajbari, ascribed to Fate Khan and Kalu Khan, now stand at the BDR (BGB) gate in Kurigram town. The age of the royal line says nothing about the age of the surviving remains (audit).
established_era: 16th century origin of the Panga line (Koch); surviving remains undated
founder_or_family: Narasimha, eldest son of the Koch founder Biswa Singha, founded the Panga line (Rangpur lineage table). Last ruled by Rani Lakshmipriya and her adopted son Debendra Narayan (district portal).
architectural_style: Unknown
preservation_status: Ruins: broken brick and a stone-paved pond, plus a nearly intact kachari (estate office) building (district portal, undated).

coordinates_note: Google Maps place 'উলিপুর মুন্সিবাড়ী (Rajbari)' (historical landmark, 59 reviews), found on 16 Oct 2026. short_description: The Munshis of Ulipur were estate officers rather than great zamindars: the Daily Star and Wikipedia trace the property to Bonwari Munshi, a surveyor under Nawab Sirajuddaula, and later to Binod Lal and Brajendra Lal Munshi, who served Maharani Swarnamoyi's Kasimbazar estate. The surviving two-storey house, dated by an inscription to about 1880, stands in a compound of about 39 acres with a Natmandir, Durga, Bishnu, Gobinda and Shiva temples, a guest house and a pond. Pakistani troops raided it in 1971 and slashed Brajendra Lal's portrait with a bayonet. The family left for Kolkata, the government took over, and a union revenue office moved in in 1987. Reports from 2017 and 2023 describe leaking roofs, stolen iron stairs and railings, and livestock tethered on the verandah. A legend says the site was chosen after a frog was seen eating a snake. The project's master list treats the book's 'Dharanibari Zamindar Bari' as this house; that identification is likely but not proven.
established_era: Mid-18th century estate; main house completed around 1880 (inscription)
founder_or_family: Bonwari (Banowari) Munshi, a surveyor under Nawab Sirajuddaula (Daily Star 2017; Wikipedia); later Binod Lal and his adopted son Brajendra Lal Munshi, who worked for Maharani Swarnamoyi of Kasimbazar
architectural_style: Two-storey domed house mixing Mughal and European styles
preservation_status: Badly decayed. Listed as a protected site of the Department of Archaeology (Ulipur portal; Wikipedia). Rooms long used by the union land office, which has since moved to a new building in the courtyard (Protidiner Sangbad, 2023).

alternate_names: Kakina Rajbari; কাকিনা জমিদারবাড়ী; Rajbari of Maharaja Mahima Ranjan
coordinates_note: Google Maps place 'Kakina Jomidar Bari' (heritage building, 50 reviews, plus code W7C2+PV4), seen in a Google Maps results list on 16 Oct 2026; coordinates to 5 decimals.
short_description: Kakina was a chakla of Cooch Behar until 1687, when the Mughal faujdar of Ghoraghat attacked Cooch Behar and Ram Narayan, who sided with him, was made chaudhuri of Kakina. The estate peaked under Shambhu Chandra (Shambhu Charan) Roy, who founded the weekly Rangpur Prakash in 1860, and his adopted son Mahima Ranjan Roy Chowdhury (1853-1909), zamindar from 1868, who founded a museum and library at Kakina, held exhibitions there in 1877 and 1879, and founded the Rangpur Sahitya Parishad in 1905 (Banglapedia). His successor Mahendra Ranjan fell into debt and the zamindari was auctioned in 1925. What remains about 200 yards west of Kakina bus stand is a four-storey hawakhana, parts of a two-storey palace, a court hall, guest house and outlying medicine house. Amar Desh reported in June 2026 that it is on the brink of collapse and that the Department of Archaeology plans an inspection. Tales of secret rooms and tunnels are local memory, not survey findings.
established_era: Estate 1687; surviving buildings undated
founder_or_family: Ram Narayan, made chaudhuri of Kakina after the Mughal campaign against Cooch Behar in 1687; later Shambhu Chandra (Shambhu Charan) Roy and his adopted son Mahima Ranjan Roy Chowdhury
architectural_style: European design with Mughal ornament (Amar Desh 2026)
preservation_status: Ruinous: roofs partly collapsed, plaster falling and walls cracked (Amar Desh, June 2026). The four-storey hawakhana is the main survivor; Bangla Wikipedia says the main building is used by Uttar Bangla College.
master_list_reference: Book row: Lalmonirhat #1, কাকিনা জমিদার বাড়ি

alternate_names: Tushbhandar Rajbari; তুষভান্ডার জমিদার বাড়ী; Ghoshal zamindar bari, Tushbhandar
coordinates_note: Google Maps place 'তুষভান্ডার জমিদারবাড়ি' (historical landmark, 108 reviews), found on 16 Oct 2026.
short_description: Murari Deb Ghoshal, a Brahmin priest from the 24 Parganas, came to Cooch Behar in the reign of Koch king Pran Narayan with the deity Rasik Roy and received land; local tradition says he paid his rent in husk (tush), which was stored east of the present house, giving Tushbhandar ('husk store') its name. The Rangpur lineage table dates the devottar estate to 1634 and says Ramdev Ghoshal bought a share of the Karjirhat chakla around 1740 and became zamindar. Kaliganj upazila is named after the later zamindar Raja Kaliprasad Roy Chowdhury of the Ghoshal family. The project's master list adds, from an older district portal page, Kaliprasad's succession in 1824 and Ramanimohan's school and dispensary of 1872. The AI-generated guide's 'Raja Girijananda Roy Chowdhury' is not supported by any source (audit), and the '400-year-old house' is really the age of the estate.
established_era: Estate 1634 (devottar), zamindari about 1740; surviving buildings undated
founder_or_family: Murari Deb Ghoshal Bhattacharya, a priest from 24 Parganas, founded a devottar estate in 1634; his descendant Ramdev Ghoshal bought a two-anna share of the Karjirhat chakla about 1740 and established the zamindari (Rangpur lineage table). Kaliprasad Roy Chowdhury, after whom Kaliganj is named, was a later zamindar.
architectural_style: Unknown
preservation_status: The house still stands (Jago24, Sept 2026); no condition survey found. The Rangpur Division heritage list names the zamindar house's Kali temple.
master_list_reference: Book row: Lalmonirhat #2, তুষভান্ডার জমিদার বাড়ি

alternate_names: Dimla Zamindar Bari; ডিমলা জমিদার বাড়ি; ডিমলা রাজবাড়ী

The family's later house in Rangpur city belongs to the Rangpur district records; this record covers only the Dimla site, which needs field confirmation.

alternate_names: Nilkuthi; নীলকুঠি; Nilphamari Officers' Club; Old DC bungalow
coordinates_note: Pin found in Google Maps on 16 Oct 2026, from the place's own pin. Matched 'Nil Kuthi-Current Officers Club' (historical landmark, 24 reviews, WVM3+8M5, Saidpur-Nilphamari Road). The club's own listing 'Officers Club Nilphamari' (WVM3+7MG) is at practically the same point.
short_description: The surviving indigo-planters' house of Nilphamari town, the district's best-documented link to the indigo trade that may have given it its name. Planters lived and ran the business here; Honorary Magistrates who punished farmers refusing to grow indigo later lived in it. It served as the Deputy Commissioner's bungalow from 1984 until 1988 and became the Officers' Club in 1999. A kuthi, the open land in front of it and part of an indigo-processing well also survive at the edge of town (Kali O Kalam 2025). The book's paragraph says Nilphamari has several nilkuthis; the district background names kuthis at Durakuti, Dimla, Kishoreganj and Tengonmari (audit).
established_era: British period; English indigo planting in the area began around 1801 (Kali O Kalam 2025). Building date not found.
founder_or_family: English indigo planters (Kali O Kalam 2025). Prothom Alo (2024) says it was built as a subdivision office.
architectural_style: British-era bungalow, about 60 x 51 ft, tin-roofed, with two fireplaces, two bedrooms, two bathrooms, a drawing room and a verandah (Kali O Kalam 2025).
preservation_status: Standing and in use as the Nilphamari Officers' Club since 12 October 1999; repaired, with a history plaque (Kali O Kalam 2025).

short_description: In Sonahar village, about 12 km from Debiganj sadar, Motilal Roy's estate once covered about 7,000 bigha. The ruined main building keeps its carved walls; beside it are a temple with Chandi and Radha-Krishna shrines, an old well, a partly ruined bathing ghat, a disused cremation ghat and another house where descendants still live. Family stories tell of elephants and a carriage shipped from Britain. Visiting the lived-in part needs permission.

architectural_style: Not described; carved wall designs survive on the main building

architectural_style: Two-storey palace facing east with about 76 m of frontage, U-shaped plan, central marble staircase and a ribbed conical dome on an octagonal neck with semi-Corinthian columns (Wikipedia)
preservation_status: Protected monument (Department of Archaeology, 1995); Rangpur Museum on the upper floor since 2005.

short_description: In Haripur town near the Indian border, the Haripur zamindars split around 1900 into two branches. The Boro Torof palace, begun by Raghavendra Roy Chowdhury and completed by his son Jagendra Narayan (1893 per the audit), is a two-storey building with floral ornament and fourteen busts of Jagendra Narayan on its east wall; a Shiva temple and natmandir stood to the east. To the west, the Chhoto Torof palace was built in 1903 for Nagendra Behari and Girija Ballabh. The AI-generated guide's claim that Ghanashyam Kundu founded the building is corrected by the audit: he is the ancestor.
established_era: 1893 for the Boro Torof palace (audit, citing the district tourist page); the district antiquities page also prints 1793. Chhoto Torof built 1903.
founder_or_family: Begun by Raghavendra (Raghabendra) Roy Chowdhury and finished by his son Jagendra Narayan Roy Chowdhury, whom the British titled Rajarshi. The family descends from Ghanashyam Kundu, a cloth trader said to have arrived around 1400 and bought part of the auctioned zamindari of the widow Meherunnesa; he is an ancestor, not the builder (district portal; audit).
architectural_style: Two-storey palace with floral plaster ornament; fourteen busts of Jagendra Narayan along the top of the east wall
preservation_status: Standing but decaying; the district portal says its remaining artefacts are nearly gone. The library and lion gate are lost.

short_description: Seat of the rajas and zamindars of Baniachong, the pargana that gave its name to what is often called the world's largest village. Govinda Singha built the first palace on the west bank of the Padmanabha (Karnakhan's) dighi near today's Upazila Parishad; Habib Khan's tomb, which Vromon Guide identifies as Govinda Singha's after his conversion, is nearby. In the 17th century Dewan Abed moved the palace to Dewan Bagh in the north of Baniachong. The grounds once had a flower garden and three gates; what remains is a scatter of ruins, bathhouses and mosques, now a popular weekend spot for photography. English Wikipedia also records Anwar Khan and Hussain Khan of Baniachong fighting the Mughals in the early 1600s.
established_era: Two seats are described. The first palace was built by Govinda Singha, ruler of Baniachong (later Habib Khan after converting to Islam); Dewan Abed moved the seat to Dewan Bagh in northern Baniachong in the 17th century (Vromon Guide, after the upazila portal). English Wikipedia dates the 'ancient Rajbari' at Puranbagh to 1737-38.
founder_or_family: Govinda Singha / Habib Khan (first palace); Dewan Abed Reza (Abed Raja), 17th-century zamindar of Baniachong pargana (later seat). Banglapedia calls Baniachong pargana's holder the only zamindar in Sylhet under the Permanent Settlement. Current custodian as heir: Ahmad Zulkar Nayin (Alokito Habiganj).
architectural_style: Mughal-style remains (Vromon Guide). Alokito Habiganj says the palace was modelled on Isa Khan's house; not confirmed.
preservation_status: Ruins. Four stone pillars and scattered stone and marble fragments remain by the dighi (Vromon Guide, 2019); about a century ago the remaining walls were removed to build a high school. Near Boro Bazar there are two bathhouses, two mosques and the ruins of an old building; the palace was burned in 1971 (Alokito Habiganj, 2022).

short_description: Jalsukha, a haor village on the Kushiyara in Ajmiriganj, was the seat of fourteen zamindars, each collecting rent from his own taluk. Most left for India after 1947. The remains are a group of houses rather than one palace: the Atchala meeting hall of Gobin Chandra Roy, said to be the most powerful of the fourteen, where the zamindars met; Kshetranath Roy's mahal, still lived in by his grandson's family; Dul Govinda Roy's house, where Lord Clive is said to have stayed and Ghetu dance was performed; Baikuntha Das's house, where the third Sri Hatta Sammilani was held; the Ghetu Nat Mandir; temples; and a stone-paved pond ghat. Chandra Kumar Roy founded Krishna Gobinda High School in 1876. Scenes of Humayun Ahmed's telefilm 'Ghetuputra Kamola' were shot here. Ajmiriganj's UNO applied in 2020 to have the houses declared a tourism site.
established_era: Described as about 250 years old (Sylhet i News, 2026). Lord Clive is said to have stayed a night at Dul Govinda Roy's house in the 18th century (Daily Sylhet News, 2020). The village school dates from 1876.
founder_or_family: Fourteen zamindar families, thirteen Hindu and one Muslim (Daily Sylhet News 2020, Sylhet i News 2026). Named: Chandra Kumar Roy, Krishna Kumar Roy, Suryamoni Roy, Baikuntha Nath Roy, Sarat Chandra Roy, Bharat Chandra Roy, Nandalal Roy, Gobin Chandra Roy, Satish Kumar Roy, Lakshmikanta Roy, Kshetranath Roy, Madhab Chandra Roy, Rama Ballav Haldar and Ramjan Ali Chowdhury (Bucha Miah Chowdhury).
architectural_style: Not described in detail. The best-known building is the Atchala, a meeting hall (baithakkhana).
preservation_status: Unprotected and mostly dilapidated; some buildings nearly gone. The Atchala's roof fell in a storm, wooden floors and furniture have been stolen, and one room is used as the land office. The tehsil office supervises the site and has asked for repairs; locals want the Department of Archaeology to take it over (Sylhet i News, Apr 2026). Some houses are occupied by former staff's descendants or local strongmen (Daily Sylhet News, 2020).

coordinates_note: Pin found in Google Maps on 14 Oct 2026. Matched place 'Prithimpassa Nawab Bari / পৃথিমপাশা নবাব বাড়ী' (Prithimpasha, Rabir Bazar, Kulaura 3233), with sub-places Nawab Bari Masjid, Nawab Bari Dighi and the family graveyard.
short_description: Seat of the Shia zamindar family of Prithimpassa in Kulaura, 47 km east of Moulvibazar town on a roughly 25-acre estate. The family's power dates from Gaus Ali Khan's 1792 jagir; his successors Ali Ahmad Khan (who built Ali Amjad's clock at Sylhet's Chandnighat in 1872-74) and Nawab Ali Amjad Khan made it one of Sylhet's leading estates, and the Shah of Iran stayed four days in 1950. The compound has old residential buildings, a large stone-banked pond, a three-domed mosque rebuilt after the 1897 earthquake (with a Sultanate-era inscribed stone) and an imambara that is the region's main Muharram venue.
established_era: Family tradition dates the founder's settlement to 1499; the British jagir dates from 1792; the palace's legacy is about 200 years old (Bangladesh Tourism Board). The present mosque is late 19th century (after the 1897 earthquake).
founder_or_family: Prithimpassa (Nawab) family, Shia nobles of Longla pargana, descended from Sakhi Salamat, a Persian from Khorasan (family history). Gaus Ali Khan received a 1,200-hal jagir from the British in 1792; Nawab Ali Amjad Khan was its best-known zamindar.
architectural_style: Brick-and-surki zamindar buildings (Wikipedia); a three-domed Mughal-style mosque of lime mortar with minarets and a red-marble floor (Daily Star 2020); a Shia imambara.
preservation_status: Family seat still in use: the imambara hosts Muharram observances and a fair each year. No report of the main buildings' condition was found; no protected-monument status confirmed. Listed by the Moulvibazar District Administration among the district's heritage sites.

name_en: Raja Subid Narayan's Rajbari (Kamala Rani Dighi)
name_bn: রাজা সুবিদ নারায়ণের রাজবাড়ি (কমলা রানীর দিঘী)
alternate_names: Kamala Rani's Dighi; Ita Rajbari
coordinates_note: Google Maps place 'Kamala Ranir Dighee / কমলা রাণীর দিঘী' (a water body), read on 14 Oct 2026. It sits on a large rectangular pond with the Rajnagar-Balaganj road along its west bank, which matches the upazila portal. This marks the dighi, not the ruins or tombs on its west bank, which have no pin. The earlier pin (24.5307223, 91.8562218) was wrong: it belongs to a modern apartment complex about 1.1 km south.
short_description: Remains associated with Raja Subid Narayan of the Ita kingdom at Uttar Gorgaon, Rajnagar, around the 12-acre Kamala Rani Dighi. Legend says the queen, Kamala Rani, vanished into the pond after worshipping the river goddess so that water would fill it; the king is said to have died of grief. The Mansurnagar Dewan family traces its descent from his son Haji Khan. The shrine of Shah Qutb Uddin with its mosque stands on the western bank. This is a pre-Mughal royal site, not a zamindar house.
established_era: Late 16th century: Subid Narayan, eldest son of Bhanu Narayan, was crowned in 1580 (Rajnagar Upazila portal); the Ita kingdom fell to Khwaja Usman in 1612 (Wikipedia).
founder_or_family: Raja Subid Narayan, last king of the Ita kingdom founded by his father Raja Bhanu Narayan.
architectural_style: Not described; only 'ruins of an ancient structure' on the dighi bank.
preservation_status: Ruins in serious disrepair on the bank of Kamala Rani's Dighi, plus the tomb ruins of the king and two sons on the western bank. The original ghat is lost; a new ghat was built on the western bank (Rajnagar Upazila portal). Listed by the Moulvibazar District Administration as a heritage site.

alternate_names: Saheb Bari; Sab Bari; সাহেব বাড়ি
coordinates_note: Google Maps place 'ভাটিপাড়া' (Heritage building, plus code V7C8+5P4), checked 14 Oct 2026. The name is only the village name, so treated as approximate. The 'Bhatipara Jomider Bari jame Mosque' place has plus code V7C8+7X8 (about 24.8707, 91.2672, beside this pin), but its marker sits 4 km away at 24.85584, 91.30746 and looks misplaced. Village pin 'Bhatipara' at 24.86968, 91.26715.
short_description: Muslim zamindar seat on the Piyain river and the haor at Bhatipara, called Saheb Bari locally. Its three-domed Zamindar Bari Jame Mosque on about 10 bigha, with a large pond in front, is the best-documented building and described as the only old mosque of its kind in the Bhati region. The master list's claims about the family's role in education and infrastructure have no source.
established_era: The family's mosque is dated to the late 17th century by BSS (2026) and Prothom Alo (2023), or to 1830 by some locals; English Wikipedia says 19th century. The house is undated.
founder_or_family: The Bhatipara zamindars, whose lands covered parts of today's Derai, Jamalganj, Shalla and Tahirpur upazilas (BSS 2026). BSS credits zamindar Fateh Mohammad Alifattaher with the mosque. The audit cites a Prothom Alo report naming the Chowdhury family; that report was not read here.
architectural_style: Not described for the house. The mosque has three large domes, 16 minarets and seven doors, in lime and surki on the model of Delhi's Jama Masjid, with white marble and ceramic floral decoration.
preservation_status: House condition not described in the sources read. The mosque is in daily use; BSS reports calls for government protection.

alternate_names: Gaurarang Zamindar Bari; গৌরারং জমিদার বাড়ী
coordinates_note: Pin found in Google Maps on 14 Oct 2026, from the place's own pin. Matched place 'Gourarong Jomidar Bari' (Historical landmark, plus code 28PQ+WQ6); a spelling variant of the name.
short_description: Hindu zamindar seat about 3 km west of Sunamganj town on roughly 30 acres. An earthquake about a century ago badly damaged the house and killed the zamindar's younger brother; in 1971 the Pakistan army destroyed the main gate and other buildings. Dol Purnima and other festivals were once held here.
established_era: Early 1800s according to local residents (Sunamganj district portal); 'about 200 years old'.
founder_or_family: The Chowdhury family of Gourarang. The district portal names Ram Govinda Chowdhury as founder; Bangla Wikipedia names Rajendra Kumar Chowdhury and Rakesh Ranjan Chowdhury in its infobox and says the estate grew most under Ram Govinda. The union portal says Rajendra Kumar and Nagendra Kumar Chowdhury managed the zamindari. The last zamindar was Nagendra Chowdhury.
architectural_style: Six separate buildings including a Rang Mahal whose walls carry relief figures of men, women and foliage, an andarmahal and a jalsa ghar; a walled bathing ghat with a 'water veranda' for the women of the house.
preservation_status: Abandoned and decaying: walls mossy, several sections collapsed, overgrown (district portal; Bangla Wikipedia). No descendants live there; Niranjan Chowdhury, Nagendra's son, lives in Sunamganj town.

alternate_names: Lakkhonsri Zamindar Bari; Lakshmansree Zamindar Bari; Hason Raja Museum, Sunamganj; লক্ষণশ্রী জমিদার বাড়ি; হাসন রাজা মিউজিয়াম; হাছন রাজার বাড়ি
coordinates_note: Pin found in Google Maps on 14 Oct 2026, from the place's own pin. Matched place 'Hason Raja museum' (Museum, plus code 39CV+J58, Sunamganj); Bangla and English searches lead to the same place. Not the 'Hason Raza Memorial' pin on the Sylhet side.
short_description: Birthplace and family home of the mystic poet and zamindar Hason Raja on the Surma at Tegharia, in Sunamganj town. The Sunamganj district portal places Hason Raja's house in Tegharia and lists the museum; English Wikipedia gives his birth on 21 Dec 1854 in Teghoriya, Lakshmansree pargana. The museum holds his clothes, sword and shield, chair and table, handwritten song manuscripts, musical instruments, a bajra boat, and the only known photograph of him. He is buried at the family graveyard at Gazir Dorga in the town. This is a different place from the Museum of Rajas at Zindabazar, Sylhet, and from the family's Rampasha seat in Bishwanath; both of those belong to the Sylhet thread.
established_era: Family estate of the Lakshmansree pargana in the 19th century; Hason Raja was born here in 1854. No construction date for the surviving buildings was found.
founder_or_family: The Dewan family of Hason Raja (Dewan Hason Raja Chowdhury, 1854-1922). His father Dewan Ali Raja managed his wife's Lakshmansree properties (English Wikipedia). The museum is run by his great-grandson Samarin Dewan (Prothom Alo 2017).
architectural_style: A three-storey and a two-storey building plus seven rooms with old-style wooden frames and tin roofs (Prothom Alo 2017). Hason Raja's own thatched house was badly damaged in the 1897 earthquake (English Wikipedia).
preservation_status: Lived in by the family; four ground-floor rooms of the three-storey building are a family-run museum (Prothom Alo 2017, about 250-300 visitors a day). Listed by the Sunamganj district portal as the Hason Raja Museum.

alternate_names: Howli Rajbari; Haoli Rajbari; Hawli Zamindar Bari; Halhalia Haoli; Laurer Garh; হাওলি রাজবাড়ি; লাউড়ের গড়
coordinates_note: Not on Google Maps; pin skipped at Orca's request after two lookups on 14 Oct 2026 (Claude, Orca's browser, read-only). Rejected: 'Halhalia fort' (25.09905, 91.17550), which is Google's Tahirpur town pin, and 'Laurer Garh Bazar' (25.18477, 91.26071), a market. Halhalia village pins are around 25.171, 91.195; no labelled ruin there.
short_description: Ruined palace of the Laur kingdom between Halhalia and Brahmangaon villages, near Tanguar Haor at the foot of the Meghalaya hills. It is a royal seat rather than a zamindar house, though Bangla Wikipedia and local reports call it a zamindar bari. During Akbar's reign the capital moved to Baniachong after Khasi raids; Gobinda Singh later restored it here. Jahangirnagar University archaeologists surveyed it in November 2017; Department of Archaeology excavation began in November 2018.
established_era: Uncertain. Local tradition (Bangla Wikipedia, Kazir Bazar) credits Raja Bijoy Singha about 1,200 years ago; the Department of Archaeology's excavators date the ruins to c. 1500-1600 AD on architectural grounds, with no inscriptions or coins found (Daily Star 2019).
founder_or_family: Rulers of the Laur kingdom, whose capital was at Halhalia. Achyut Charan Choudhury (1920, via Daily Star) says Umed Raja, a descendant of Gobinda Singh (Habib Khan), built the haoli or rajbari in the 16th century.
architectural_style: Ruins of a walled palace compound of about 30 acres: main gate, a pond with stone steps, boundary walls and large structural mounds. Sources mention a lion gate, prison, dance hall and durbar hall that are no longer visible.
preservation_status: Declared a protected archaeological site (Laurer Garh) on 25 Sep 2019. Excavation has been slow and about 70-80 families have built on the land (Natun Sylhet, March 2023). The Department of Archaeology planned an open-air museum (Daily Star 2019).

alternate_names: Pailgaon Chowdhury Bari; Babur Bari; পাইলগাও জমিদার বাড়ি; বাবুর বাড়ি
coordinates_note: Pin found in Google Maps on 14 Oct 2026, from the place's own pin. Matched place 'Pailgaon Jomidar Bari' (Historical landmark, MHW3+VXF, Jomidar Bari Road, Pailgaon 3060, Jagannathpur).
short_description: Seat of the Chowdhurys of Pailgaon on about 5.5 acres by the Kushiyara. Brajanath Chowdhury's son Sukhamoy chaired Sylhet municipality (1916-26) and founded Pailgaon Brajanath High School (1919); Brajendra Narayan founded what is now Sylhet Government Women's College. Locals call it Babur Bari. The Department of Archaeology proposed protection after the family's descendants appealed at the school's centenary in January 2020.
established_era: Estate lineage said to be over 300 years old (district portal); the surviving complex was built 1913-1921 (Bangladesh Pratidin 2021).
founder_or_family: The Pailgaon Chowdhurys: Kanailal Dhar married into the old Pal family of the village; Umananda Dhar (Binod Roy) received the Chowdhury title from Mughal emperor Muhammad Shah; in 1786 four brothers enlarged the estate under the Decennial Settlement (Daily Star 2021). Brajanath Chowdhury raised it to a leading zamindari; his grandson Brajendra Narayan Chowdhury, Sylhet Congress president and Assam legislator, was the last zamindar. The surviving buildings were made by mistri Dhanjan Raj.
architectural_style: Kachari building with many doors beside a large pond, a bungalow with an earthen roof, a bhog mandir, family quarters, guard quarters and a small prison cell in a thick wall; a second pond with a stone-paved bank.
preservation_status: Declared a protected archaeological site by the Ministry of Cultural Affairs on 21 Jan 2021 (Daily Star). Abandoned since the family left; bricks falling, roofs damaged, kachari overgrown (Bangladesh Pratidin, June 2021).

alternate_names: Panail Dewan Bari; পানাইল দেওয়ান বাড়ি
coordinates_note: The house is not on Google Maps (checked 14 Oct 2026). Coordinates are the compound's mosque, 'Panaeel Jomidar Bari Jame Mosque' (Mosque, plus code 2HH3+3JG), which Bangla Wikipedia places in the family compound. Village pin 'Panail' at 25.01195, 91.54265; not used.
short_description: Seat of the Dewan family of Dohalia pargana, known locally as Dewan Bari, with buildings called Rajbari, Dewan Bari and Zamindar Bari. The family line split into Hindu and Muslim branches in the 16th century. The graveyard holds Dewan Mohammad Ahbab and Dewan Mohammad Azraf. The only description found is Bangla Wikipedia's article, based on a 2018 Daily Sylheter Dak feature by Muhammad Habibul Helali.
established_era: Family tradition: Raja Srimanta Roy settled here c. 1381; the surviving gate and mosque are said to be about 400 years old (Bangla Wikipedia, citing Daily Sylheter Dak 2018).
founder_or_family: Raja Srimanta Roy, said to have come from Rajputana. Prem Narayan Roy reportedly became Muslim in 1581 as Raja Mohammad Islam; Raja Mohammad Masum was made dewan of Dohalia pargana under Alivardi Khan. Later members include the anti-British zamindar Kushal Roy Chowdhury, Dewan Mohammad Ahbab Chowdhury and the philosopher and National Professor Dewan Mohammad Azraf.
architectural_style: Brick, lime and surki. A gate said to be about 400 years old, a family mosque, Dewan Manzil and a family library; the main two-storey house fell in the 1897 earthquake.
preservation_status: Gate, mosque and family graveyard survive; little upkeep. Family members still live there, though most of the wider family is abroad (Bangla Wikipedia).

alternate_names: Sukhair Rajapur Zamindar Bari
coordinates_note: No zamindar-bari place on Google Maps; pin skipped at Orca's request after two lookups on 14 Oct 2026 (Claude, Orca's browser, read-only). 'Razapur jomidar bari' (24.87433, 90.97972) is in Mohanganj town, Netrokona, so not this site. 'Rajapur SYED BARRI, Dharmopasha' (Historical landmark, 24.88685, 91.10564, about 9 km south of Sukhair) has nothing tying it to the zamindars; not used.
short_description: A branch seat of the Sukhair zamindars in the neighbouring village of Rajapur. Bangla Wikipedia lists 'Rajapur Zamindar Bari' among Dharmapasha's notable heritage sites, and the official Sukhair history explains how the branch began. No source describes a surviving house, so this record is held as a lead until someone identifies the building.
established_era: After Pratap Roy Chowdhury, fourth in line from Mahamanikya Datta of Sukhair, took half the Sukhair estate; probably 18th century (inferred, not stated by any source).
founder_or_family: Pratap Roy Chowdhury, who married into a Muslim family of Rajapur, converted to Islam and became zamindar of Rajapur (Bangla Wikipedia's Dharmapasha page; the upazila portal tells the same story).
architectural_style: Unknown
preservation_status: Unknown. No source describes the building.
