alternate_names: Sukhair Rajbari; Sukair Zamindar House; সুখাইড় রাজবাড়ি; Rajmahal of the haor
coordinates_note: Pin found in Google Maps on 14 Oct 2026, from the place's own pin. Matched place 'সুখাইড় জমিদার বাড়ি,সুনামগঞ্জ' (Heritage building, plus code X49H+HXG).
short_description: Haor-country seat of the Roy Chowdhury zamindars at the foot of the Meghalaya hills, on the north bank of the Ghagla-jur, about 35 km from Sunamganj town and 18 km from Dharmapasha. The estate held some 20 jalmahals (Dhankunia, Charda and others) and is linked locally to the 1922 Nankar rebellion and to a story of a zamindar shooting three tigers to save an English officer in Tanguar Haor. A fourth-generation descendant, Pratap Roy Chowdhury, became Muslim and took half the estate as zamindar of Rajapur next door (see rajapur-zamindar-bari-dharmapasha).
established_era: Land bought c. 1691; building begun 1695 and finished over several generations (Dharmapasha Upazila portal; Kalbela 2026).
founder_or_family: Mahamanikya Datta Roy Chowdhury, who bought a jagir at Sukhair c. 1691 while travelling from Hooghly to Assam; his descendant Mohanlal began the house in 1695. The Financial Express (2026) names Rajib, Mohanlal and Keshab Roy Chowdhury as builders. The last zamindar was Bimal Chandra Roy Chowdhury, 'Chhana Babu' (c. 1918-2004), per Bangla Wikipedia.
architectural_style: Multi-courtyard brick complex; of the four sections of the main courtyard, the Bara Bari, Majham Bari and Chhoto Bari survive in part, with a bungalow, kachari, jalsa ghar, storehouse and khas kamra (Kalbela 2026; Rupali Bangladesh 2026). Known locally as the 'Rajmahal' of the haor.
preservation_status: On the verge of collapse: cracked walls and failing roofs and plaster (Kalbela, Rupali Bangladesh, Sept 2026). The Dharmapasha UNO says a conservation proposal has gone to the ministry and the Department of Archaeology is aware. Descendants (Mohan Chowdhury) still live there and keep about 25 acres.

alternate_names: Kamakhya Babur Bari; Rajapur Zamindar Bari
coordinates_note: Not on Google Maps (searched twice on 14 Oct 2026 in Orca's browser). Two Google places named 'Babur Bari' fall in Sylhet Sadar and Kulaura, so they are not this house. Shivsagar Dighi, which lies south of the house (Samakal, Prothom Alo), has no pin either. Village pin for Maijgaon, not the house: 24.6861248, 91.9512937.
short_description: A rare Assam-type wooden zamindar house at Rajapur in Fenchuganj, built in 1331 BS by zamindar Jayanarayan Dev Choudhury. The compound also has a Vishnu temple with a Garuda column, a guest house, granaries, a kachari and Shivsagar Dighi. Not on the project's master list; found while researching Sylhet District.
established_era: Built in 1331 BS (about 1924-25), about 101 years before the 2025 report.
founder_or_family: Zamindar Jayanarayan Dev Choudhury; named after his son Jitendra Narayan Dev Choudhury 'Kamakhya' (Prothom Alo 2025).
architectural_style: Two-storey Assam-type wooden house of six rooms with a tin roof bearing three tin peacocks, narrow verandas and iron railings brought from Kolkata.
preservation_status: Still habitable but ageing: veranda floorboards are loose and some features are deteriorating. The main house is usually locked while the family, most of whom live abroad, is away; caretakers keep up the temple (Prothom Alo, Sep 2025).

alternate_names: Jaintia Rajbari; জৈন্তা রাজবাড়ি; Jaintapur Rajbari
coordinates_note: Pin found in Google Maps on 14 Oct 2026, from the place's own pin. Matched place 'Jaintia Rajbari' (historical landmark, plus code 44PG+P7 Jaintapur). The Wikipedia infobox pin (25.133783, 92.121704) is about 500 m south-west, so the two do not agree.
short_description: Seat of the Jaintia kings in the plains below the Jaintia Hills, about 43 km from Sylhet city on the Tamabil road. The brick palace dates from the 18th century, and the British annexed the kingdom's plains territory in March 1835 under Raja Rajendra Singh. The site stands about 1 km east of the upazila bus stand, on a hillock north of the road and about 200 m west of the upazila complex's main gate (Daily Star Bangla 2025). Locals often confuse it with Jaintiaswari Bari, the separate temple house of the kings' deity in the upazila centre, which has a stone well, a circular sacrificial platform and murals conserved by the Department of Archaeology.
established_era: The plains capital of the Jaintia kingdom from at least the 15th century (Daily Star 2015). The surviving brick palace was built about 1731-1770 (Daily Star Bangla 2025); an earlier palace was of stone.
founder_or_family: The Jaintia (Pnar/Sinteng) kings. Daily Star Bangla (2025) credits the brick palace to Raja Bar Gosain II, with construction overseen by his nephew and commander Fateh Khan.
architectural_style: Brick palace with Mughal influence, the first Jaintia palace built of brick (Daily Star Bangla 2025); set inside a decorated brick enclosure wall with megaliths around it (Daily Star 2015).
preservation_status: Largely lost. Daily Star Bangla (Mar 2025) says parts were demolished for a madrasa and the upazila complex now occupies part of the grounds; only an old pond and a walled temple with its well remain clearly visible. The 2015 Daily Star describes a gate, enclosure wall and throne building. Department of Archaeology protection for the palace itself was not confirmed (the audit says the department lists the megalithic tombs and Jaintiaswari Bari).

alternate_names: Konung Leikai; Sanggai-yumpham; Mirza Jungle Rajbari
coordinates_note: Pin found in Google Maps on 14 Oct 2026. Matched place 'Manipuri rajbari' (historical landmark, VVV7+R3, Mirza Jangal Rd).
short_description: Residence built in exile by the Meitei princes of Manipur after the Burmese invasion drove them to Sylhet. The complex, Sanggai-yumpham in Konung Leikai, was walled in seven rings of brick. Raja Gambhir Singh, who later retook Manipur, also built the Tin Mandir at nearby Lamabazar in 1826, which still stands. Not on the project's master list; it is a royal residence, not a zamindar house.
established_era: Early 19th century; work began about 1824, during Manipur's 'Seven Years' Devastation' (1819-1826) (Wikipedia).
founder_or_family: The exiled Meitei princes of Manipur: Raja Gambhir Singh (Wikipedia); Daily Star Bangla (2025) names the three brothers Chourjit, Marjit and Gambhir Singh.
architectural_style: Palace complex enclosed by seven brick walls of brick and surki, with a multi-storey royal gate (Sanathong) about 4 m high (Wikipedia).
preservation_status: In ruins. About three-quarters has disappeared (Daily Star Bangla 2025). Surviving: wall sections (one about 22 m long and 2.5 m high), two gate openings, the Sanathong gate, part of a rear gate and one of two ponds; the queens' pond has been filled. Manipur's Mutua Museum repaired one royal gate in 2012 (Wikipedia).

name_en: Museum of Rajas' (Hason Raja Museum), Zindabazar
alternate_names: Hason Raja Museum & Palace (master list); Raja-Kunjo; রাজা-কুঞ্জ
coordinates_note: Google Maps place 'Museum of Rajas'' (museum, VVV8+VV, 808 Jallarpar Rd), read on 14 Oct 2026, agrees within about 25 m with the Wikipedia infobox (24.8949, 91.8673).
short_description: Folk museum of the Raja family of Sylhet, centred on the mystic poet Dewan Hason Raja (1854-1922), at Raja-Kunjo in Zindabazar. It has two galleries: family objects and photographs, a large collection of folk instruments, props from the 2002 film Hason Raja, and furniture and books of the poet's son Dewan Eklimur Raja. Wikipedia says the museum occupies Hason Raja's former town home; the audit says the government source it read does not establish that, so this is recorded as a museum, not a palace.
established_era: Museum opened 30 June 2006; the building is described as about a hundred years old (Wikipedia).
founder_or_family: Educationist Dewan Talibur Raja Trust, named for Hason Raja's grandson (Wikipedia; audit citing a government PDF).
architectural_style: Tin-roofed house of several rooms with a front piazza (Wikipedia).
preservation_status: In use as a museum.

name_en: Rampasha Zamindar Bari (Hason Raja's ancestral home)
name_bn: রামপাশা জমিদার বাড়ি (হাসন রাজার পৈতৃক বাড়ি)
alternate_names: Hason Raja's house, Rampasha; হাসন রাজার বাড়ি, রামপাশা
coordinates_note: Pin found in Google Maps on 14 Oct 2026. Matched place 'Hason Raza Memorial' (historical place, plus code VP4G+WPF); a second place 'Hason Raza Museum' sits 25 m away (24.8569383, 91.7268078). Neither is named as the house itself, so this marks the family site at Rampasha. Not to be confused with the Hason Raja museum in Sunamganj town.
short_description: Ancestral home of the zamindar family of Dewan Hason Raja, the Sylheti mystic poet, at Rampasha in Bishwanath. Hason Raja himself was born and raised at Teghoria in Lakshmansree pargana (now Sunamganj), where his father managed his mother's estate, about 33 miles from Rampasha; that birthplace is a separate record kept by the Sunamganj thread. The Rampasha house stands beside a large pond within the old zamindari lands and draws visitors daily, but has been left uncared for.
established_era: Not dated. The family held the Rampasha zamindari by the mid-19th century; Hason Raja was born in 1854.
founder_or_family: The Raja family of Rampasha: Dewan Ali Raja, father of the mystic poet Dewan Hason Raja (1854-1922), grandson of Birendraram Singhadev (Wikipedia, Hason Raja).
architectural_style: Described only as a village house or bungalow beside a large pond (Daily Star 2013); no architectural description found.
preservation_status: Neglected. The Daily Star (2013) and Financial Express (2019) report the house and pond in poor repair, waste dumped in the pond, and attempts to grab adjacent land; locals want it made a tourist site. No later report was found.

alternate_names: Borobari; Atgram Chowdhury Bari; Sajid Raja'r bari
coordinates_note: Pin found in Google Maps on 14 Oct 2026. Matched place 'দেওয়ান সাজিদ রাজার বাড়ি' (historical landmark, plus code X9MW+5W8). 'Atgram Boro Bari Masjid' is next door (24.982525, 92.3976744); its listing does not say it is the multi-domed mosque.
short_description: Seat of the Dewan (Chowdhury) family of Atgram, whose landholdings spread across Zakiganj, Kanaighat and Karimganj. Ehsan Raja and then Sajid Raja held a court of justice from the dalan. Sajid Raja built a school, madrasa, hospital, post office, bazaar, ponds and a dak bungalow (demolished in 1971), and the multi-domed mosque in front of the house, which survived the 1897 earthquake that cracked the dalan. The Kajalshar Union portal lists the mosque at Sajid Raja's house as the union's main tourist spot and says it is reached north-east from Atgram bus station on the Sylhet-Zakiganj road. The audit flagged this as an omission from the master list.
established_era: 18th-19th century. The family settled at Atgram in the 18th century; the Borobari mansion dates to about the 1800s (family website).
founder_or_family: Dewan Ehsan Raja, a landlord from Jaintapur who settled at Atgram with his father Dewan Shah Mohammed (d. 1872); his son Dewan Sajid Raja (d. 1903) built up the estate and village (family website).
architectural_style: Mansion (Borobari), a dalan used as the family's court, a 'terochali' (13-roof) bungalow and a multi-domed mosque in front; no independent architectural description found.
preservation_status: Restored by the family: the mosque in 2016 and the house in 2023, 'almost back to its former state' (family website, not independently checked).
